Justification

Comprehensive Re-evaluation

Definitive Melanoma Identity

The cluster unequivocally represents melanoma cells based on extremely high expression of melanocyte lineage markers: Dct (98.76%), Tyrp1 (99.14%), Tyr (79.82%), Sox10 (87.21%), Gpnmb (99.36%), and Mlph (84.8%). Additionally, canonical melanoma markers are expressed at appropriate levels: MCAM (71.71%) and S100B (51.99%) are both robustly expressed, confirming melanoma identity. The melanocyte transcription factor MITF (44.35%) is also present. The absence of immune (Cd3e 0.32%, Cd68 9.17%), endothelial (Pecam1 1.38%), and fibroblast markers (Col1a1 1.82%, Vim 0.0%) definitively excludes non-tumor cell types.

Addressing the Thymocyte Prediction

The C2S-Scale prediction of "thymocyte" is biologically implausible and represents a computational artifact. Critical thymocyte markers are essentially absent: Cd3e (0.32%), Cd3d (0.27%), Cd4 (0.38%), Cd8a (0.2%), Rag1 (0.04%), Rag2 (0.03%), Ptcra (0.0%), Cd24a (0.24%), and Thy1 (0.0%). These values are at or near background levels. The tissue context is 100% tumor tissue from melanoma samples, not thymus. The thymocyte prediction likely results from algorithmic misinterpretation of stress response signatures or metabolic reprogramming patterns that superficially resemble developing lymphocytes.

Neural Crest Reprogramming Features - A Critical Finding

The feedback correctly identifies a neural crest-like reprogramming signature that was underappreciated in the previous annotation:

Strong neural crest/neuronal markers:

  • PAX3 (80.04%) - a master neural crest transcription factor, extraordinarily high
  • APP (74.53%) - amyloid precursor protein, neuronal
  • RTN4 (79.65%) - reticulon 4/Nogo, axonal growth inhibitor
  • TUBB3 (ranked #33) - neuronal class III β-tubulin
  • FUS (73.46%) - RNA-binding protein, neuronal function
  • TARDBP (72.32%) - TDP-43, RNA-binding protein
  • MAPT (33.84%) - microtubule-associated protein tau
  • NCAM1 (27.18%) - neural cell adhesion molecule

Weak neural crest stem markers:

  • SNAI2 (5.24%) - low but present
  • SOX9 (4.39%) - low
  • Other canonical neural crest markers (Foxd3, Twist1, Pax7) are essentially absent

This pattern suggests neural crest lineage reprogramming rather than true neural crest stemness. Melanoma cells derive from neural crest and can reactivate neural crest programs under stress. The high PAX3 expression is particularly striking, as PAX3 is a key neural crest specifier that is normally silenced in differentiated melanocytes but can be reactivated in melanoma, especially under stress conditions. The RNA-binding proteins (FUS, TARDBP) and neuronal cytoskeletal proteins (TUBB3, MAPT) suggest a stress-adaptive phenotype with neuronal-like features, potentially related to invasive or migratory capacity.

Complete MHC-I Silencing and Immune Evasion

The feedback highlights complete absence of MHC-I components: B2M (0.0%), H2-K1 (0.0%), H2-D1 (0.0%). This is a critical finding indicating active immune evasion through MHC-I downregulation, preventing CD8+ T cell recognition. This is a well-documented melanoma immune escape mechanism and is highly relevant to the C57 genotype context (96% of cells). The moderate expression of immune checkpoint molecules (Cd274/PD-L1 16.92%, Cd47 17.88%) combined with complete MHC-I loss represents a multi-layered immune evasion strategy.

Mitochondrial Dysfunction - Warburg Effect Extreme

The feedback correctly identifies catastrophic mitochondrial gene collapse:

Absent mitochondrial genes:

  • Pyruvate dehydrogenase: PDHA1 (0.0%), PDHB (0.0%), DLAT (0.0%)
  • TCA cycle: ACO2 (0.0%), SUCLG1 (0.0%), SUCLG2 (0.0%), MDH1 (0.0%), MDH2 (0.0%)
  • Electron transport chain: UQCRC1 (0.0%), COX5B (0.0%), CYCS (0.0%), COX4I1 (0.0%), COX6C (0.0%), NDUFA1 (0.0%)
  • ATP synthase: ATP5A1 (0.0%), ATP5B (0.0%), ATP5G1 (0.0%)

Present mitochondrial genes (partial function):

  • TCA cycle enzymes: CS (84.95%), OGDH (53.44%), IDH1 (28.52%), IDH2 (62.87%), FH1 (23.84%)
  • Complex I: NDUFS1 (76.06%)
  • Complex II: SDHA (55.77%), SDHB (91.27%)

This pattern indicates selective mitochondrial dysfunction with preservation of some TCA cycle enzymes (likely for biosynthetic precursor generation) and early electron transport components, but complete loss of terminal oxidative phosphorylation machinery. This represents an extreme Warburg effect - near-total reliance on glycolysis despite oxygen availability. The preserved TCA cycle enzymes may support reductive carboxylation for lipid synthesis and other anabolic processes rather than ATP generation.

Extreme Glycolytic Reprogramming

The comprehensive glycolytic signature remains the most prominent feature: Pgk1 (99.06%), Aldoa (99.86%), Pkm (98.77%), Tpi1 (95.82%), Gpi1 (95.64%), Pfkl (93.79%), Hk2 (89.9%), Hk1 (83.2%), Ldha (82.78%), Eno1 (70.94%), Pfkp (97.53%). This is consistent with the mitochondrial dysfunction and represents metabolic adaptation to support rapid proliferation and survival under stress.

Stress Response Integration

The ER stress and ISR activation remain valid: ATF4 (95.57%), ATF5 (92.51%), DDIT3 (86.32%), HSPA5 (87.42%), P4HB (99.27%), ERO1L (97.64%), TRIB3 (83.48%). The hypoxic adaptation is supported by: VEGFA (84.3%), SLC16A3 (91.08%), SLC2A1 (71.79%), DDIT4 (79.9%), HIF1A (51.85%).

Proliferative and Oncogenic Features

Moderate proliferation markers (MKI67 50.82%, TOP2A 59.83%, CDK2 86.31%) and oncogenic drivers (MYC 83.28%, CCND1 59.54%, BRAF 11.11%, NRAS 9.13%, KRAS 25.72%) confirm active tumor cell cycling. The expression of survival factors (BCL2 10.48%, BIRC5 34.09%) and invasion-associated genes (FN1 58.01%, ITGB1 94.81%, CD44 52.73%) supports an aggressive phenotype.

Why Not Neuroblastoma or Glioblastoma?

Despite neural features, this is not neuroblastoma or glioblastoma-like:

  • Neuroblastoma markers are absent: PHOX2B (0.01%), DBH (0.02%), TH (0.01%)
  • Mature neuronal markers are absent: NEFL (0.0%), NEFM (0.01%), SNAP25 (0.02%), SYN1 (0.08%)
  • The melanocyte lineage markers (DCT, TYRP1, TYR, GPNMB) are incompatible with neuroblastoma or glioblastoma
  • The neural features represent lineage plasticity within melanoma, not transdifferentiation to another tumor type

Synthesis: A Multifaceted Melanoma Phenotype

This cluster represents melanoma cells with:

  1. Definitive melanoma identity (DCT, TYRP1, SOX10, MCAM, S100B)
  2. Neural crest reprogramming (PAX3, APP, RTN4, TUBB3, FUS, TARDBP) - stress-adaptive lineage plasticity
  3. Complete MHC-I silencing (B2M, H2-K1, H2-D1 absent) - immune evasion
  4. Mitochondrial dysfunction (terminal OXPHOS genes absent) - extreme Warburg effect
  5. Glycolytic dominance (comprehensive glycolytic enzyme expression)
  6. Integrated stress response (ER stress, hypoxia, ISR activation)
  7. Proliferative activity (moderate cycling markers)

Annotation Decision

The annotation remains "Melanoma Cell" because the melanocyte lineage markers are definitive and incompatible with other cell types. However, the granular annotation is revised to acknowledge the neural crest reprogramming and mitochondrial dysfunction. The neural crest features represent phenotypic plasticity within melanoma rather than a distinct cell type, and are likely adaptive responses to the tumor microenvironment that enhance survival, invasion, and immune evasion. This phenotype is consistent with aggressive, therapy-resistant melanoma subtypes that exhibit lineage plasticity and metabolic flexibility.

Review Comments

Expert Assessment Integration

The five expert assessments converge on a unified, sophisticated interpretation of this cluster as a highly adapted melanoma cell state, not a heterogeneous mixture. The complete absence of MHC-I components (B2M, H2-K1, H2-D1 at 0%) is universally confirmed and recognized as a deliberate immune evasion strategy, not an artifact. This is functionally coupled with the upregulation of PD-L1 (16.92%) and CD47 (17.88%), forming a coordinated checkpoint axis that enables tumor survival despite interferon pathway activation. The neural crest reprogramming signature—PAX3 (80.04%), TUBB3 (85.52%), FUS (73.46%), TARDBP (72.32%)—is not interpreted as transdifferentiation but as stress-induced phenotypic plasticity. All experts agree these markers reflect hijacking of neuronal effector programs for invasion and survival, consistent with melanoma's neural crest origin. The preservation of key mitochondrial enzymes like SDHB (91.27%), NDUFS1 (76.06%), CS (84.95%), and OGDH (53.44%) is consistently noted as evidence of targeted metabolic rewiring for biosynthesis, not random collapse.

Biological Context

This phenotype emerges within the C57 genotype context, where tumor-intrinsic stress responses are amplified by microenvironmental pressures such as hypoxia and nutrient limitation in dense tumor cores. The extreme glycolytic flux—driven by near-universal expression of HK2, LDHA, PKM, and PGK1—fuels rapid proliferation while bypassing dysfunctional mitochondria. The co-expression of ER stress markers ATF4 and HSPA5 with PAX3 suggests that proteotoxic stress directly triggers transcriptional reprogramming via the integrated stress response (ISR). This creates a self-reinforcing loop: stress induces plasticity genes; plasticity enhances invasion into hostile niches; invasion exacerbates metabolic stress; further stress reinforces the program.

Confidence & Heterogeneity Considerations

The High confidence assessment is robustly justified: every expert independently validated the core lineage identity through definitive markers and rejected all alternative cell type hypotheses with equal rigor. The heterogeneity status as False is equally sound—the cluster exhibits transcriptional coherence across functional modules. The "conflicting" signals are not noise but interconnected adaptations orchestrated by master regulators like ATF4/ATF5/DDIT3, which simultaneously upregulate glycolysis, suppress OXPHOS/MHC-I, and activate neuronal effectors to create a single adaptive phenotype optimized for immune evasion, metabolic autonomy, and invasive potential.

Alternative Interpretations

One plausible alternative is that this represents a pre-metastatic state where cells acquire migratory competence before dissemination: PAX3-driven cytoskeletal remodeling via TUBB3/MAPT may facilitate intravasation; MHC-I loss prevents immune detection during circulation; preserved SDHB could support succinate-mediated epigenetic silencing of metastasis suppressors. Another interpretation posits that FUS/TARDBP act as RNA chaperones stabilizing transcripts encoding pro-survival proteins under ER stress—a mechanism linking post-transcriptional control to transcriptional reprogramming previously unappreciated in melanoma biology.

Biological Significance

This cluster defines a clinically relevant subtype of therapy-resistant melanoma characterized by lineage plasticity-enabled immune evasion. The integration of neural crest reprogramming with mitochondrial rewiring creates a cell that is simultaneously invisible to T cells yet metabolically autonomous under hypoxia—a dual advantage that explains resistance to both immunotherapy and targeted therapies targeting BRAF or MEK. The preservation of SDHB/NDUFS1 suggests potential vulnerabilities: inhibiting succinate dehydrogenase or Complex I might disrupt redox balance or epigenetic regulation without triggering compensatory apoptosis seen in total mitochondrial inhibition. This phenotype underscores that aggressive melanoma is not merely a disease of oncogenic mutations but of adaptive cellular reprogramming driven by microenvironmental stress.

Cluster Context

The cluster consists of cells from tumor tissue (100%), predominantly under the "c57" condition (96%) and genotype (96%), derived from sample "output-XETG00045__0059973__c57__20250725__091031" (96%) in sample folder "4" (96%) and run "20250725__090712__Tuany_mSkinMelanoma5k_run1" (100%). Segmentation methods include 74% by interior stain (18S) and 25% by boundary stain (ATP1A1+CD45+E-Cadherin). Sample IDs show 61% from "output-XETG00045__0059973__c57__20250725__091031_0" and 34% from "output-XETG00045__0059973__c57__20250725__091031_1". Clustering metadata indicates 99% in leiden_0.5 cluster "3", 88% in leiden_1 cluster "8", and 97% in leiden_1.5 cluster "6".
In differential analysis, this cluster exhibits strong upregulation of gene expression and transcription processes (NES > 6.8), including RNA Polymerase II transcription and generic transcription pathways, indicating heightened transcriptional activity relative to other clusters. Cellular responses to stimuli and stress are prominently enriched (NES > 6.6 and 5.8), alongside immune system and innate immune pathways (NES ~5.0), suggesting robust responsiveness to environmental cues. Cell cycle regulation, particularly mitotic phases, shows moderate to strong upregulation (NES ~5.6 and 4.6), pointing to proliferative activity. Metabolism-related pathways, such as general metabolism and protein metabolism, are upregulated (NES > 4.5), with glycolysis specifically enriched in WikiPathways (NES 4.13). In contrast, GPCR signaling pathways are strongly downregulated (NES < -5.3 for ligand binding and -4.7 for Class A rhodopsin-like receptors), including amine ligand-binding receptors (NES -3.57), highlighting reduced G protein-coupled receptor activity. Synaptic processes, including inhibitory synapse assembly (NES -4.03) and action potential membrane depolarization (NES -3.94), are downregulated, consistent with singleSample findings of GABAergic transmission suppression (NES < -4.4). Dendritic cell migration and chemotaxis display significant downregulation (NES < -3.85), indicating diminished migratory behavior. Keratinization and related epithelial processes, such as cornified envelope formation (NES -4.0), are also suppressed, alongside striated muscle contraction (NES -3.75). Signaling by Rho GTPases is upregulated (NES > 4.8), potentially compensating for downregulated GPCR pathways through alternative cytoskeletal regulation. These patterns, supported by high NES across GO, Reactome, and WikiPathways, underscore cluster-specific transcriptional activation and immune responsiveness contrasted with reduced signaling and structural assembly processes.

Disease Association

This cluster represents an aggressive, therapy-resistant melanoma subtype characterized by three interrelated pathological hallmarks: neural crest reprogramming, complete MHC-I silencing, and catastrophic mitochondrial dysfunction. The definitive melanoma identity is confirmed by high expression of lineage markers (DCT, TYRP1, SOX10, MCAM), while the reactivation of neural crest transcription factors (notably PAX3) and neuronal cytoskeletal proteins (TUBB3, MAPT) indicates a stress-induced phenotypic plasticity that enhances invasive potential and immune evasion. This is not a distinct tumor type but rather a dedifferentiated state within melanoma pathogenesis. The complete absence of MHC-I components (B2M, H2-K1, H2-D1) represents a primary immune escape mechanism that prevents CD8+ T cell recognition—a hallmark of advanced melanoma resistant to checkpoint inhibitors. This is compounded by upregulation of alternative immune checkpoints like PD-L1 and CD47. The most striking feature is the near-total collapse of oxidative phosphorylation machinery with preservation of glycolytic enzymes and partial TCA cycle components (CS, OGDH), indicating an extreme Warburg effect adapted for biosynthetic support rather than ATP production. This metabolic reprogramming is directly linked to ER stress (HSPA5, ATF4) and hypoxia signaling (VEGFA, SLC2A1). Together, these features define a highly aggressive phenotype associated with poor prognosis in cutaneous melanoma (DOID:8923) and potentially with the rare syndrome of melanoma-neural system tumor predisposition due to CDKN2A mutations (DOID:0111511). Therapeutically, this cluster suggests vulnerability to agents targeting glycolysis (e.g., LDHA inhibitors), ER stress pathways (e.g., IRE1α modulators), or immune restoration strategies such as NK cell engagers to bypass MHC-I loss.

Therapeutic Approach

This melanoma cell cluster represents an aggressive, therapy-resistant phenotype characterized by neural crest reprogramming (PAX3, TUBB3, APP), complete MHC-I silencing (B2M, H2-K1 absent), and catastrophic mitochondrial dysfunction with extreme glycolytic dependency. The most clinically relevant therapeutic approach is immune checkpoint blockade with pembrolizumab, an FDA-approved anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody that targets the PD-L1 pathway upregulated in this cluster (16.92% expression). Despite MHC-I loss, pembrolizumab may still exert efficacy by reactivating CD8+ T cells and NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity against PD-L1+ tumor cells. However, the profound immune evasion necessitates combination strategies: agents targeting the ER stress response (e.g., IRE1α inhibitors under preclinical investigation) could disrupt survival signaling driven by ATF4 and HSPA5, while LDHA inhibitors—though not yet FDA-approved—are emerging as promising metabolic disruptors to exploit the cluster's absolute dependence on glycolysis (PGK1, PKM, LDHA >90% expression). Safety considerations include immune-related adverse events from checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., colitis, hepatitis) and potential neurotoxicity risks due to neuronal protein expression (TARDBP, FUS), warranting neurological monitoring. Future opportunities include NK cell engagers to bypass MHC-I loss and dual targeting of glycolysis and ER stress pathways. This molecular profile aligns with poor-prognosis melanoma subtypes resistant to conventional therapies but offers actionable vulnerabilities for precision oncology approaches.

Justification

Re-evaluation of Annotation Based on Feedback

Critical Assessment of Neuronal Marker Expression

The feedback raises important concerns about the high expression of neuronal/neural crest markers (APP 95.83%, RTN4 15.21%, RTN3 16.3%, TARDBP 14.58%, FUS 9.87%). However, upon careful re-examination, these markers do NOT support a neural crest-derived hybrid or perineural invasion interpretation:

APP (Amyloid Precursor Protein) - 95.83%:

  • While APP is known for its role in neurons, it is actually a ubiquitous transmembrane protein expressed in many cell types
  • APP functions in cell adhesion, cell-matrix interactions, and growth regulation in epithelial cells
  • High APP expression in epithelial cells is well-documented and not specific to neural lineages
  • The biological context notes that APP is among "ubiquitous and housekeeping genes" in this dataset
  • APP expression at 95.83% in cluster 6 vs 47.04% in other clusters suggests enrichment but not exclusive neural identity

RTN4, RTN3, TARDBP, FUS - All LOWER in cluster 6 than other clusters:

  • RTN4: 15.21% (cluster 6) vs 28.16% (other clusters) - DEPLETED
  • RTN3: 16.3% (cluster 6) vs 31.02% (other clusters) - DEPLETED
  • TARDBP: 14.58% (cluster 6) vs 26.97% (other clusters) - DEPLETED
  • FUS: 9.87% (cluster 6) vs 23.77% (other clusters) - DEPLETED

This is the opposite of what would be expected for neural crest-derived or perineural cells. These markers are actually relatively suppressed in cluster 6 compared to the rest of the dataset, arguing strongly AGAINST a neural/neural crest identity.

Keratin Absence: Technical vs Biological Explanation

The complete absence of keratins (Krt5, Krt14, Krt15 all at 0%) is indeed unusual, but the data shows:

  • Krt5, Krt14, Krt15 are 0% in ALL clusters (other_clusters_mean = 0.0)
  • This indicates keratins are not in the Xenium gene panel, not that this cluster specifically lacks them
  • This is a technical limitation of the spatial transcriptomics platform, not a biological absence

The Xenium platform uses a targeted gene panel, and keratins were apparently not included. This does not invalidate the basal epithelial identity when all other evidence supports it.

Overwhelming Evidence for Basal Epithelial Identity

Master Regulator (Highly Enriched):

  • Trp63: 26.37% (cluster 6) vs 12.66% (other clusters) - 2.1-fold enriched
  • Trp63 is THE definitive transcription factor for basal epithelial cell identity
  • No other cell type expresses Trp63 at this level

  • Lamb3: 12.57% vs 1.67% - 7.5-fold enriched - laminin-332
  • Lama3: 14.65% vs 4.4% - 3.3-fold enriched - laminin-332

  • Dsc3: 25.87% vs 12.24% - 2.1-fold enriched - desmocollin-3

  • Plec: 42.56% vs 36.1% - 1.2-fold enriched - plectin

Rejection of Alternative Hypotheses

Neural Crest-Derived Hybrid Cells - REJECTED:

  • Neural crest markers Sox10 (1.53% vs 14.72%) and Mitf (1.96% vs 9.97%) are DEPLETED
  • Melanocyte markers Tyrp1 (4.27% vs 24.19%) and Dct (4.49% vs 23.99%) are DEPLETED
  • RTN4, RTN3, TARDBP, FUS are all DEPLETED compared to other clusters
  • No evidence of neural crest signature

Perineural Stromal Cells - REJECTED:

  • Fibroblast markers are absent or depleted: Vim (0%), Sparc (0%), Pdgfra (0.85% vs 3.84%), Pdgfrb (1.46% vs 11.06%)
  • Strong epithelial junction proteins (Dsp, Jup, Dsc3) are incompatible with stromal identity
  • No perineural-specific markers present

Fibroblasts - REJECTED:

  • Complete absence of Vim (0%) and Sparc (0%)
  • Col1a1 (3.21% vs 11.87%) and Col1a2 (24.42% vs 45.81%) are DEPLETED
  • Strong epithelial markers incompatible with mesenchymal identity

Melanoma Cells - REJECTED:

  • All melanoma markers are depleted: Sox10, Mitf, Tyrp1, Dct all lower than other clusters
  • Mlana and Pmel are 0% (not in panel)
  • Expression profile is epithelial, not melanocytic

EMT Cells - REJECTED:

  • Mesenchymal markers absent: Vim (0%), S100a4 (0%), S100a6 (0%)
  • EMT transcription factors very low: Twist1 (0.13%), Snai1 (0.4%), Zeb1 (0.26%)
  • Strong epithelial junction proteins indicate stable epithelial phenotype

Addressing C2S-Scale Predictions

The feedback mentions C2S-Scale predictions of "thymocyte, fibroblast" conflicting with the annotation. However:

  • Automated cell type prediction tools can be inaccurate, especially with spatial transcriptomics data
  • The absence of keratins from the gene panel would confuse automated classifiers
  • The actual marker expression overwhelmingly supports basal epithelial identity
  • Thymocyte prediction is clearly incorrect (no T cell markers)
  • Fibroblast prediction is incorrect (no Vim, Sparc, depleted collagens)

Heterogeneity Status

The feedback notes heterogeneity status is "True," suggesting multiple populations. However:

  • The consistent enrichment of basal epithelial markers across the cluster suggests a coherent identity
  • Heterogeneity may reflect different states (quiescent vs primed) or locations (interfollicular vs follicular) within the basal epithelial compartment
  • There is no evidence of distinct subpopulations with fundamentally different identities (e.g., some cells epithelial, others neural)

Biological Context Integration

The cluster is 100% from tumor tissue in melanoma samples. The most parsimonious explanation is:

  • These are normal basal epithelial cells from skin structures (epidermis or hair follicles) present within or adjacent to melanoma tissue
  • The quiescent state (very low Mki67, Pcna, Top2a) suggests these are reserve stem cells
  • The hair follicle markers (Sox9, Hr, Fgf18, Nfib) suggest these may be hair follicle-associated basal epithelial cells
  • APP overexpression may reflect stress response or microenvironmental signaling in the tumor context

Conclusion

After careful re-evaluation of the feedback, the evidence strongly supports maintaining the basal epithelial cell annotation:

  1. Neuronal markers are NOT overexpressed - RTN4, RTN3, TARDBP, FUS are all depleted; APP is ubiquitous
  2. Keratin absence is technical - keratins are not in the Xenium panel (0% in all clusters)
  3. Basal epithelial markers are massively enriched - Trp63, Itgb4, Col7a1, Lamb3, Lama3, Epcam, Trim29, Aqp3 all show 2-7 fold enrichment
  4. Complete hemidesmosome signature - pathognomonic for basal epithelial cells
  5. All alternative hypotheses are rejected by the data

The annotation remains Basal Epithelial Cell with high confidence, specifically representing quiescent basal epithelial cells with hair follicle-associated characteristics, likely from normal skin structures within the melanoma microenvironment.

Review Comments

Expert Assessment Integration

The five expert assessments converge on a unified biological narrative: this cluster represents a quiescent hair follicle-associated basal epithelial stem cell embedded within the melanoma microenvironment. All experts independently validated the core annotation through convergent evidence—Trp63 (26.37%), Itgb4 (28.46%), Col7a1 (19.68%), Lamb3 (12.57%), and Lama3 (14.65%) form an unambiguous hemidesmosome signature exclusive to basal epithelial anchoring. The enrichment of Sox9 (25.38%), Hr (25.11%), and Fgf18 (10.58%)—each exceeding 5-fold over other clusters—confirms a follicular bulge identity, not general epidermal basal cells. Critically, all experts dismissed neural crest contamination: while APP is highly expressed (95.83%), the neuronal markers RTN4, RTN3, TARDBP, and FUS are depleted in this cluster compared to others, confirming APP’s role as an epithelial adhesion molecule under stress, not a neural lineage indicator.

Biological Context

This population resides within tumor tissue but exhibits no melanoma-specific markers; instead, it mirrors normal skin architecture co-opted into the tumor niche. The extreme suppression of proliferation genes (Mki67 1.81%, Pcna 2.76%) and global transcriptional machinery aligns with reserve stem cell quiescence observed in murine hair follicle bulges during homeostasis. Paradoxically, GPCR signaling is upregulated: ADCY1, FZD1, FGFR2, and FGFR3 are enriched 4- to 7-fold, suggesting active reception of paracrine signals from neighboring immune or stromal cells—likely Wnt or FGF ligands from PD-L1+ immune infiltrates. Yet canonical downstream effectors like NF-κB are suppressed: NFKB1 (3.7% vs 6.07%) and RELA (1.74% vs 5.83%) are downregulated despite Pdl1_cre dominance, indicating active suppression of inflammatory feedback loops to preserve stem cell integrity under chronic immune pressure.

Confidence & Heterogeneity Considerations

Confidence remains High due to unanimous expert agreement on structural markers and rejection of alternatives. The heterogeneity status is correctly labeled False: there is no evidence of multiple lineages within this cluster. The apparent "heterogeneity" noted in some reviews stems from misinterpretation of single markers—not distinct subpopulations. For example, elevated APP does not indicate neural hybridity; it reflects stress adaptation common to quiescent epithelial niches. Similarly, suppressed CD274 (PD-L1) at 0.68% versus 7.98% elsewhere confirms these cells do not actively engage immune checkpoints—they are passive architectural components whose presence correlates with tumor invasion rather than drives immune evasion.

Alternative Interpretations

One plausible alternative is that these cells represent senescent keratinocytes undergoing metabolic rewiring to survive microenvironmental stress. Their preserved adhesion machinery with suppressed transcriptional activity mirrors senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) without inflammation—a state consistent with high Lmna expression (nuclear stiffness) and low cell cycle gene expression. Another interpretation posits they are epithelial bystanders captured spatially near tumor nests but functionally inert; however, their specific molecular signature—including Fgf18-driven signaling and Sox9 maintenance—is too precise for random sampling. A third possibility involves partial reprogramming by tumor-derived signals—but absence of oncogenic drivers like Myc or Ras pathway activation argues against transformation.

Biological Significance

This cluster reveals a critical mechanism of tumor tolerance: the co-option of resilient, non-proliferative epithelial niches that provide structural stability without provoking immune responses. By maintaining hemidesmosomes and desmosomes without keratins (a technical artifact), these cells preserve tissue architecture while avoiding proliferative signals that could trigger anti-tumor immunity. Their upregulated GPCR signaling may facilitate communication with stromal fibroblasts or dendritic cells via non-canonical pathways, potentially promoting immunosuppressive myeloid recruitment through CXCL14 without direct PD-L1 engagement. This suggests melanoma tumors exploit pre-existing skin stem cell compartments as inert scaffolds rather than transforming them—a paradigm shift from conventional models of tumor cell plasticity. Future studies should validate whether these cells serve as reservoirs for post-therapy regeneration or contribute to resistance against targeted therapies aimed at proliferative populations.

Cluster Context

This cluster comprises cells exclusively from tumor tissue (100%), with genotype and condition distributions dominated by Pdl1_cre at 43%, followed by Pdl1_wt at 20% and c57 at 17%. Sample folder compositions show 43% from folder "10", 20% from "1", and 17% from "4". All cells originate from the single run "20250725__090712__Tuany_mSkinMelanoma5k_run1". Segmentation methods include 58% using interior stain (18S) and 40% using boundary stain (ATP1A1+CD45+E-Cadherin). Specific sample IDs contribute with 14% from "output-XETG00045__0059973__Pdl1_cre__20250725__091031_2" and 12% from "output-XETG00045__0059973__Pdl1_cre__20250725__091031_3". Clustering assignments indicate 97% alignment to leiden cluster "2" at resolution 0.5, 97% to "5" at resolution 1, and 98% to "5" at resolution 1.5.
In differential analysis, this cluster exhibits strong downregulation of cell cycle processes (NES < -5.0 for Cell Cycle, Mitotic Cell Cycle, G1/S Transition, and related checkpoints), indicating reduced proliferative activity relative to other clusters. Transcriptional regulation is markedly suppressed, with high-confidence downregulation in Gene Expression (Transcription) (NES -5.72), RNA Polymerase II Transcription (NES -5.15), and Generic Transcription Pathway (NES -4.72). Immune system pathways are significantly downregulated (NES -5.63 for Immune System; NES -3.97 for Innate Immune System), alongside reduced activity in cellular responses to stimuli (NES -5.30) and stress (NES -5.00). Metabolism-related processes show consistent downregulation, including Metabolism of Proteins (NES -5.26), Metabolism of RNA (NES -4.60), and Glycolysis and Gluconeogenesis (NES -4.31 from WikiPathways). In contrast, GPCR signaling is upregulated, with strong enrichment in GPCR Ligand Binding (NES 4.78) and Class A (Rhodopsin-like Receptors) (NES 4.34), complemented by GPCRs Non-Odorant (NES 3.97 from WikiPathways). TRAF6-mediated NF-κB activation is moderately upregulated (NES 3.78), suggesting enhanced inflammatory signaling potential. Single-sample analysis reveals absolute upregulation of Immune System (NES 4.15) and Signaling by Rho GTPases (NES 3.91), though these are relatively suppressed in differential comparisons. Viral and infectious disease pathways are downregulated (NES < -4.8), highlighting diminished pathogen response capabilities. Overall, the cluster displays a profile of quiescence in proliferation and broad metabolic/transcriptional activities, with selective enhancement in GPCR-mediated signaling.

Disease Association

This cluster represents quiescent basal epithelial cells with a complete hemidesmosome signature (Trp63+, Itgb4+, Col7a1+, Lamb3+, Lama3+), likely derived from normal skin structures such as hair follicles or interfollicular epidermis embedded within the melanoma tumor microenvironment. While basal epithelial cells themselves are not malignant, their presence in melanoma tissue is biologically significant. Basal cell carcinoma (DOID:2513) is the primary disease directly associated with neoplastic transformation of basal epithelial cells, characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of Trp63-expressing cells. However, in this context, the cluster is quiescent and lacks proliferative markers, indicating it is not transformed but rather a non-neoplastic component of the tumor stroma. The overexpression of APP—a protein implicated in both neuronal function and epithelial adhesion—may reflect microenvironmental stress or aberrant signaling from adjacent melanoma cells. The downregulation of immune pathways suggests these basal cells may be shielded from immune surveillance, potentially contributing to an immunosuppressive niche that supports melanoma progression. The enrichment of hair follicle stem cell markers (Sox9, Lgr5, Fgf18) implies these may represent a reservoir of stem-like epithelial cells whose dysregulated interactions with melanoma could influence tumor invasion or resistance to therapy. Therapeutically, preserving or modulating this basal compartment might offer novel strategies to disrupt tumor-stroma crosstalk without targeting the cancer cells directly.

Therapeutic Approach

This cluster consists of quiescent basal epithelial cells with a definitive hemidesmosome signature (Trp63+, Itgb4+, Col7a1+, Lamb3+, Lama3+), embedded within the melanoma tumor microenvironment. While no FDA-approved drugs directly target Trp63 or the hemidesmosomal complex, therapeutic strategies can be inferred from their biological roles. Integrin β4 (Itgb4) is a key mediator of epithelial-stromal adhesion and signaling; preclinical studies suggest that inhibiting α6β4 integrin disrupts tumor-stroma crosstalk in squamous cell carcinomas and may sensitize tumors to chemotherapy. In melanoma, preserving this quiescent basal compartment could be beneficial, as its downregulation of immune pathways may contribute to an immunosuppressive niche—suggesting that immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., anti-PD-1/PD-L1) may indirectly modulate its behavior by altering cytokine gradients. APP overexpression, while not neuronal in origin here, may reflect stress-induced signaling; drugs targeting amyloid processing (e.g., BACE inhibitors) are investigational but not indicated for skin contexts. Safety considerations include avoiding broad-spectrum cytotoxics that may damage normal epithelial stem cells, potentially impairing wound healing or promoting scarring. Emerging opportunities include targeted delivery of FGF18 or SOX9-modulating agents to regulate hair follicle stem cell quiescence, thereby disrupting tumor-supportive stromal niches without inducing proliferation. Additionally, spatially guided therapies using nanocarriers to deliver TGF-β inhibitors specifically to this compartment may prevent melanoma invasion along basement membrane interfaces. This cluster represents a non-malignant but functionally critical component of the tumor microenvironment; future therapies should aim to reprogram rather than eliminate it.

Justification

Evidence Analysis and Final Decision

Overview

This cluster represents melanoma cells - the malignant tumor cells in this melanoma tissue dataset. The annotation integrates evidence from multiple hypotheses, with strongest support for Hypothesis 1 (Proliferative melanoma cells) and Hypothesis 2 (Stressed melanoma cells with ER stress response), while rejecting hypotheses suggesting stem-like or dedifferentiated phenotypes.

Key Supporting Evidence

Melanocyte Lineage Identity

The cluster shows unambiguous melanocyte lineage identity through robust expression of core melanocyte markers:

  • Gpnmb (rank 1), Tyrp1 (rank 2), Dct (rank 5), Tyr (rank 13) - all critical melanin synthesis pathway genes
  • Sox10 (rank 10) and Pax3 (rank 27) - master melanocyte transcription factors
  • Mitf (52.72%), Oca2 (20.00%), Slc45a2 (62.85%), Mc1r (55.42%) - additional melanocyte differentiation markers
  • Mlph (rank 18) and Rab38 (rank 29) - melanosome transport genes

This comprehensive melanocyte signature definitively identifies these as melanoma cells (malignant melanocytes) rather than any other cell type in the tumor microenvironment.

Proliferative State

Hypothesis 1 is strongly supported by exceptional proliferation markers:

  • Mki67 (64.98%), Pcna (56.25%) - canonical proliferation markers at very high frequencies
  • Ccnd1 (66.21%), Birc5 (33.80%), Aurkb (37.61%) - cell cycle regulators
  • Cell cycle genes in marker list: Hist2h2bb (rank 6), Cdk2 (rank 12), Dnmt1 (rank 20), Top2a (rank 28), Anln (rank 9), Myc (rank 39)
  • Pathway enrichment: cell cycle processes (NES 6.15) - the highest enrichment score

This indicates these melanoma cells are actively cycling, representing the proliferative tumor cell population driving melanoma growth.

ER Stress and Adaptive Response

Hypothesis 2 provides critical context about the cellular state:

  • ER stress markers: Atf4 (76.02%), Ddit3 (25.87%), Eif2ak3 (26.16%)
  • Chaperones and protein folding: Hspd1 (rank 3), Canx (rank 4), P4hb (rank 16), Hspa5 (rank 41), Calu (rank 31)
  • CCT chaperonin complex: Cct7 (rank 8), Cct5 (rank 21), Cct3 (rank 22), Cct8 (rank 49)
  • Pathway enrichment: cellular responses to stress (NES 5.20), protein metabolism (NES 5.65), post-translational modifications (NES 5.12)

The ER stress response is selective (absence of Xbp1, Hyou1, Pdia4) but robust, indicating melanoma cells are managing proteotoxic stress while maintaining high proliferation - a characteristic of aggressive tumor cells adapting to microenvironmental challenges.

Rejection of Alternative Hypotheses

Hypothesis 3 (Stem-like features) - REJECTED

While Sox10, Pax3, Myc, and Ctnnb1 are present, canonical stem cell markers are completely absent:

  • Cd133 (0.00%), Abcb5 (0.00%), Aldh1a1 (0.00%), Nestin (0.00%), Cd271 (0.12%), Jarid1b (0.00%)
  • Sox2 (0.04%), Nanog (0.00%), Pou5f1 (0.00%)

The genes supporting this hypothesis (Sox10, Pax3) are core melanocyte lineage markers, not stem cell markers. Their presence reflects melanocyte identity, not stemness.

Hypothesis 5 (Amelanotic/dedifferentiated) - REJECTED

This hypothesis is strongly contradicted by the robust melanocyte differentiation signature:

  • Complete melanin synthesis pathway intact: Tyrp1, Dct, Tyr, Mitf, Oca2, Slc45a2, Mc1r
  • EMT markers largely absent: Twist1 (0.06%), Zeb1 (0.59%), Vim (0.00%)

These are differentiated melanoma cells maintaining melanocytic identity, not dedifferentiated cells.

Hypothesis 4 (Immune-activated) - PARTIAL SUPPORT

While interferon response genes are present (Stat1 55.69%, Irf1 38.19%, Tap1 38.26%, Isg15 54.77%, Cd274 16.68%, Cxcl10 rank 35), this represents a secondary feature rather than the primary identity. The immune activation is likely a response to the tumor microenvironment in this PD-L1/immune checkpoint study context, but the cells are fundamentally melanoma cells, not immune cells.

Integration and Biological Context

The cluster shows:

  1. 100% tumor tissue origin with specific genotype distribution (38% Oprl1_cre, 38% Pdl1_cre, 22% c57)
  2. Downregulation of differentiation pathways (keratinization NES -4.69, FGFR signaling NES -4.0 to -4.4) while maintaining melanocyte identity
  3. Upregulation of immune system pathways (NES 5.31, innate immune NES 5.05) consistent with tumor-immune interactions
  4. Absence of contaminating cell types: all negative markers for T cells, B cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and keratinocytes are near zero

Conclusion

This cluster represents proliferative melanoma cells (Hypothesis 1) with ER stress adaptation (Hypothesis 2) and interferon response (Hypothesis 4 as secondary feature). The cells maintain strong melanocytic differentiation while exhibiting high proliferative activity and stress adaptation, characteristic of aggressive melanoma tumor cells in the tumor microenvironment. The granular annotation captures the proliferative state, key melanocyte markers (GPNMB, TYRP1), active melanin synthesis, and ER stress response as the most specific characterization possible.

Review Comments

Expert Assessment Integration

The five expert assessments converge on a unified core identity—this cluster is unequivocally composed of melanoma cells—but diverge profoundly on the biological mechanisms sustaining this state. The melanocyte lineage identity, anchored by near-universal expression of GPNMB (99.82%), TYRP1 (99.42%), and DCT (96.95%), is validated across all experts and confirmed by expression lookup data, ruling out contamination or misannotation. However, the functional interpretation varies: the Melanocyte Lineage Biologist identifies a paradoxical co-expression of pigmentation and interferon-response genes as an aberrant adaptive state; the Developmental Biologist frames this as a developmentally arrested melanoblast-like phenotype with suppressed FGFR/WNT signaling; the Immunometabolism Specialist highlights the disconnect between ER stress markers and absent metabolic transporters (e.g., SLC7A11), questioning the mechanism of proliferation; the Pathologist notes the silent PD-L1 transgene despite genotype assignment as evidence of epigenetic silencing; and the Spatial Immunologist interprets this as a self-sustaining signaling hub using RHOA/RAC1-driven motility to bypass GPCR dependence.

Biological Context

This cluster exists within a PD-L1/OPRL1-driven tumor microenvironment where immune pressure is high, yet these cells exhibit no classical immune evasion via surface PD-L1 protein upregulation in all contexts (CD274 = 16.68%, but transgene = 0%). The interferon signature (STAT1 55.69%, ISG15 54.77%, CXCL10 74.16%) is non-canonical: MX1 and OAS1 are completely absent (0%), suggesting activation via NF-κB or autocrine JAK-STAT loops rather than IFNAR signaling—a hallmark of stress-induced 'pseudo-immune' reprogramming rather than T-cell-mediated inflammation. The co-expression of neuronal markers (APP 64.69%, TARDBP 66.46%, FUS 69.62%) reflects retained neural crest developmental programs intrinsic to melanoma lineage plasticity, not stromal contamination, aligning with recent findings that aggressive melanomas reactivate neurodevelopmental pathways for survival.

Confidence & Heterogeneity Considerations

Confidence remains High because every expert independently affirms the primary identity and core stress-proliferation axis; discrepancies are mechanistic nuances—not contradictory identities. Heterogeneity is correctly assessed as False: while experts debate whether cells are 'differentiated', 'arrested', or 'reprogrammed', they agree these are not distinct subpopulations but rather a single population exhibiting multifaceted adaptation under oncogenic and microenvironmental pressure. Low OCA2 (20%) expression does not indicate heterogeneity—it suggests functional bottlenecking in melanosomal maturation within an otherwise uniform population undergoing proteotoxic overload.

Alternative Interpretations

An alternative model posits that these cells are not merely stressed proliferators but are actively rewiring their transcriptional network to function as autonomous signaling units: ER stress drives ATF4-mediated upregulation of ISGs and chaperones simultaneously with suppression of differentiation signals (FGFRs), creating a self-reinforcing loop that maintains proliferation while evading immune surveillance through CXCL10-induced T-cell exhaustion without requiring PD-L1 expression on their surface. This may represent a novel 'stress-adapted immune-excluded' phenotype unique to spatially dense tumor cores.

Biological Significance

This cluster exemplifies how aggressive melanomas exploit developmental plasticity to survive microenvironmental hostility. By maintaining pigment synthesis machinery for camouflage or redox balance while deploying ER stress responses to sustain proliferation under proteotoxic load—and by hijacking neurodevelopmental pathways for motility without chemotactic cues—these cells achieve autonomy from both growth factor dependence and immune recognition. The silent PD-L1 transgene suggests tumors can evade genetic reporter systems through epigenetic mechanisms, complicating therapeutic monitoring. Critically, this phenotype challenges conventional classification schemes that equate differentiation loss with aggressiveness; here, extreme malignancy is coupled with preserved lineage identity, revealing that melanoma's deadliest variants may be those most faithful to their origin yet most radically adapted.

Cluster Context

This cluster consists entirely of cells from tumor tissue, with 100% derived from a single sequencing run (20250725__090712__Tuany_mSkinMelanoma5k_run1). The sample composition shows 38% from Oprl1_cre condition and genotype, 38% from Pdl1_cre, and 22% from c57, corresponding to specific sample outputs dated 20250725__091031. Segmentation methods include 66% using interior stain (18S) and 33% using boundary stain (ATP1A1+CD45+E-Cadherin). Sample folders are distributed as 38% from folder 2, 22% from folder 4, and 38% from folder 10. Within clustering resolutions, 97% of cells belong to leiden_0.5 cluster 1, 87% to leiden_1 cluster 7, and 98% to leiden_1.5 cluster 2. Sample IDs are primarily from output-XETG00045__0059973__Oprl1_cre__20250725__091031_0 (20%), output-XETG00045__0059973__Oprl1_cre__20250725__091031_1 (18%), output-XETG00045__0059973__Pdl1_cre__20250725__091031_3 (38%), and output-XETG00045__0059973__c57__20250725__091031_2 (13%), with minor variations.
In differential analysis, this cluster exhibits strong upregulation of cell cycle processes (NES 6.15) and gene expression via transcription (NES 5.93), alongside immune system activation (NES 5.31) and cellular responses to stress (NES 5.20), indicating high proliferative and adaptive activity. Metabolism of proteins (NES 5.65) and post-translational modifications (NES 5.12) are also prominently upregulated, supporting robust cellular maintenance. Conversely, GPCR ligand binding (NES -5.16) and class A rhodopsin-like receptor signaling (NES -4.89) are strongly downregulated, suggesting reduced responsiveness to extracellular ligands. Developmental pathways such as keratinization (NES -4.69), striated muscle contraction (NES -4.62), and nephron development (NES -4.56) show significant downregulation, as do FGFR-mediated signaling cascades (NES around -4.0 to -4.4), implying diminished growth factor-driven differentiation. In GO terms, negative regulation of glial cell differentiation (NES -5.08), dendritic cell migration (NES -4.59), and synaptic transmission processes (NES -4.57) are enriched, highlighting suppression of neural and immune migratory functions. WikiPathways reveal downregulation of various GPCR classes (NES -3.6 to -4.7), inflammatory responses (NES -3.55), and lipid metabolism pathways like eicosanoid and retinol metabolism (NES -3.77 and -3.77), with consistent themes of reduced signaling and metabolic homeostasis. Single-sample analysis corroborates upregulation of innate immune system (NES 5.05) and cell cycle mitotic (NES 4.91), reinforcing cluster-specific proliferative signatures. Overall, high-confidence enrichments (NES > |4.5|) point to a profile favoring proliferation and stress adaptation over differentiation and ligand-mediated signaling.

Disease Association

This cluster represents highly proliferative, GPNMB- and TYRP1-positive melanoma cells exhibiting a robust endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress response, placing them squarely within the context of aggressive cutaneous melanoma (DOID:8923). These cells maintain core melanocytic differentiation markers (MITF, SOX10, TYR, DCT) while simultaneously activating proliferative (MKI67, PCNA, CCND1) and proteostatic stress pathways (ATF4, HSPA5, P4HB), indicating an adaptive state that supports tumor growth under microenvironmental pressure. The ER stress signature is not merely a bystander effect but a key driver of survival in melanoma, enabling these cells to manage high protein synthesis demands from rapid proliferation and oncogenic signaling while resisting apoptosis. This phenotype is clinically associated with therapy resistance and poor prognosis, particularly in tumors with BRAF or NRAS mutations where ER stress pathways are co-opted to sustain viability. The concurrent upregulation of interferon-response genes (STAT1, IRF1, CXCL10) and PD-L1 (CD274), consistent with the study's PDL1_cre genotype context, suggests these proliferative melanoma cells are actively engaging with the immune microenvironment—potentially contributing to immune evasion through PD-L1 upregulation and recruitment of immunosuppressive elements. This dual identity—proliferative and stressed—defines a dominant tumor cell state in advanced melanoma that is refractory to conventional therapies but vulnerable to agents targeting the unfolded protein response (e.g., IRE1α inhibitors) or combining immunotherapy with ER stress modulators. No other disease ontology terms show specific association with this precise combination of proliferation + ER stress + melanocytic identity; thus, cutaneous melanoma remains the primary and most biologically coherent disease association.

Therapeutic Approach

The identified melanoma cell cluster exhibits a highly proliferative, GPNMB/TYRP1-positive phenotype with robust endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and interferon response signatures, consistent with aggressive, therapy-resistant cutaneous melanoma. The most clinically relevant therapeutic agents are immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, including pembrolizumab and nivolumab—both FDA-approved for advanced melanoma. These monoclonal antibodies block PD-1 on T cells, reversing PD-L1-mediated immune evasion by tumor cells, which is directly supported by the cluster's high CD274 (PD-L1) expression and its enrichment in PDL1_cre genotypes. Mechanistically, these drugs restore cytotoxic T cell activity against proliferating melanoma cells, leading to durable responses in a subset of patients, particularly those with high tumor mutational burden or interferon-gamma signature—a feature mirrored here through STAT1, IRF1, and CXCL10 upregulation.

Therapeutic efficacy is further enhanced by combining checkpoint blockade with agents targeting ER stress pathways. Although no FDA-approved IRE1α inhibitors exist yet, investigational compounds such as MKC-3946 and STF-083010 show preclinical promise in disrupting the IRE1α-XBP1 arm of the unfolded protein response (UPR), which is hyperactivated in these stressed melanoma cells. By inhibiting this adaptive survival pathway, such agents could sensitize tumors to immunotherapy and overcome resistance mechanisms driven by proteotoxic stress. The cluster’s high expression of HSPA5, ATF4, and P4HB validates this as a druggable vulnerability.

Safety considerations include immune-related adverse events (irAEs) from checkpoint inhibitors—such as colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, and endocrinopathies—which may be amplified in patients with underlying autoimmune predispositions or high baseline inflammation. The presence of GPNMB+ melanoma cells also raises potential concerns for ocular toxicity with anti-PD-1 therapies due to shared antigen expression in uveal tissue. Monitoring for elevated liver enzymes, thyroid dysfunction, and dermatologic reactions is essential. Additionally, combination strategies involving ER stress modulators require careful toxicity profiling to avoid exacerbating hepatic or pancreatic stress responses.

Emerging opportunities include next-generation therapies: bispecific antibodies engaging both PD-1 and novel targets like LAG-3 (e.g., relatlimab-pembrolizumab combinations), mRNA vaccines targeting neoantigens derived from mutated TYRP1 or GPNMB, and CAR-T cells engineered against melanoma-associated antigens. Biomarker-guided approaches using ATF4 or HSPA5 expression levels could stratify patients for UPR-targeted therapy. Spatial transcriptomics data from this study further supports developing localized delivery systems (e.g., nanoparticle-conjugated inhibitors) to target tumor cores while sparing stromal compartments. This integrated strategy—combining immunotherapy with targeted stress modulation—represents a precision medicine paradigm for aggressive melanoma subtypes defined by proliferation-stress coactivation.

Justification

Comprehensive Re-evaluation Based on Feedback

Investigation of Feedback Points

1. Gja1-High Expression and Epithelial Co-expression

The feedback raised concern about extreme Gja1 expression (88.85%) potentially indicating two subpopulations: true ORSCs with gap junction coupling versus mis-segmented stromal/glial cells. Investigation confirms true ORSC identity: Gja1-high cells co-express strong epithelial junction markers Dsp (77.21%), Jup (63.85%), Cdh1 (50.97%), and Epcam (43.07%). All mesenchymal/stromal markers are absent: Vim (0%), S100a4 (0%), with fibroblast markers depleted (Pdgfra 1.66%, Pdgfrb 2.4%). Glial markers are also absent: Gfap (0.06%), Aqp4 (0.04%), Aldh1l1 (0.32%). The high Gja1 expression co-localizes with epithelial identity, ruling out stromal/glial contamination. This pattern is consistent with adaptive gap junction coupling in hair follicle stem cells, which use Gja1 (connexin43) for intercellular communication within the stem cell niche.

2. Ectopic Slc15a1/Ace2 Expression and NRF2 Activation

The feedback suggested investigating whether Slc15a1 (48.18%) and Ace2 (40.23%) co-localize with TXNIP or represent stress-induced transcriptional noise via NRF2. Investigation reveals stress response signature: Txnip is highly expressed (30.75% vs 19.48% in other clusters), indicating oxidative stress response. However, NRF2 pathway components show mixed patterns: Nfe2l2 is actually depleted (5.59% vs 13.35%), Keap1 is reduced (2.27% vs 4.34%), Hmox1 is depleted (4.04% vs 13.18%), while Nqo1 shows modest enrichment (1.88% vs 0.82%). This pattern suggests stress-induced transcriptional dysregulation rather than canonical NRF2 activation. The Slc15a1/Ace2 expression likely represents aberrant transcription in the tumor microenvironment context, possibly related to metabolic stress or tumor-adjacent tissue adaptation, rather than true intestinal identity.

3. C2S-Scale Thymocyte Prediction and T-cell Markers

The feedback highlighted that C2S-Scale predicts 'thymocyte' and requested investigation of T-cell markers. Investigation definitively rules out T-cell identity: All T-cell markers are absent or dramatically depleted: CD3E (0.07% vs 0.55%), CD2 (0.01% vs 0.46%), TRAC (0%), TRBC1 (0%), TRBC2 (0%), CD4 (0.01% vs 0.51%), CD8A (0%), CD8B (0%). The C2S-Scale prediction is a technical artifact, likely due to shared SOX9 expression between thymocytes (where SOX9 regulates T-cell development) and hair follicle stem cells (where SOX9 maintains stem cell identity). This represents computational cross-prediction rather than biological reality.

4. Absence of MCAM/S100B/SOX10

The feedback noted that MCAM, S100B, and SOX10 were computationally identified as markers but are not expressed here. Investigation confirms their absence supports the annotation: MCAM (3.57% vs 13.94%), S100B (1.81% vs 5.79%), and SOX10 (1.03% vs 14.73%) are all depleted in this cluster. These markers are characteristic of melanocytic lineage (SOX10, S100B) and pericytes/vascular cells (MCAM). Their absence is expected and appropriate for outer root sheath cells, which are epithelial in origin and distinct from neural crest-derived melanocytes. This absence strengthens rather than weakens the ORSC annotation.

Confirmation of Original Annotation

After addressing all feedback points, the evidence strongly supports maintaining the original annotation as outer root sheath cells:

Core Identity Markers (Unchanged)

  • Sox9 (47.02% vs 4.49%): 10-fold enrichment, definitive hair follicle stem cell marker
  • Lrig1 (23.05% vs 4.30%): 5-fold enrichment, quiescent hair follicle stem cell marker
  • Trp63 (36.77% vs 12.37%): Basal epithelial progenitor marker
  • Hr (37.61% vs 11.30%): Hair follicle cycling regulator
  • Gas1 (34.11% vs 7.34%): Growth arrest marker supporting quiescent state

Epithelial Junction Complex (Validated)

The co-expression of Gja1 with epithelial markers confirms true epithelial identity:

  • Dsp (77.21%), Jup (63.85%), Dsc3 (45.03%): Desmosomal proteins
  • Cdh1 (50.97%), Epcam (43.07%): Epithelial adhesion molecules
  • Gja1 (88.85%): Gap junction protein for stem cell niche communication

Quiescent State (Confirmed)

  • Mki67 (1.69% vs 16.17%): Minimal proliferation
  • Pathway analysis: Strong downregulation of cell cycle, mitotic phases, G2/M transition
  • Consistent with hair follicle bulge stem cells in quiescent niche

Biological Context (Validated)

  • 100% tumor tissue origin: Residual normal hair follicle structures within melanoma samples
  • Melanomas arise from hair follicle-associated melanocytes
  • Normal skin appendages commonly captured in tumor dissections

Resolution of Conflicting Evidence

Slc15a1/Ace2 Expression

Now understood as stress-induced aberrant transcription in tumor microenvironment rather than intestinal identity. The absence of all intestinal markers (Vil1, Alpi, Fabp2, Krt8, Krt18 all 0%) and presence of strong epithelial hair follicle markers confirms this interpretation.

Gja1 High Expression

Now understood as adaptive gap junction coupling in hair follicle stem cell niche, co-expressed with epithelial markers, not indicative of stromal/glial contamination.

C2S-Scale Thymocyte Prediction

Now understood as computational artifact due to shared SOX9 expression between different developmental contexts, definitively ruled out by absence of all T-cell markers.

Absence of Krt15/Krt19/Cd34

Remains a limitation but does not override the overwhelming evidence. These markers are specific to the bulge region, while outer root sheath cells exist throughout the follicle with heterogeneous marker expression. Sox9 and Lrig1 are more broadly expressed in hair follicle stem cells.

Updated Granular Annotation

The granular annotation is updated to explicitly include Gja1-mediated gap junction coupling, which is now understood as a biologically relevant feature of the stem cell niche rather than a conflicting marker.

Conclusion

After comprehensive investigation of all feedback points, the annotation as Outer Root Sheath Cells is strongly validated. The feedback concerns have been resolved:

  1. Gja1-high cells are true epithelial ORSCs with gap junction coupling
  2. Slc15a1/Ace2 represent stress-induced aberrant transcription, not intestinal identity
  3. C2S-Scale thymocyte prediction is a technical artifact with no T-cell marker support
  4. Absence of MCAM/S100B/SOX10 appropriately distinguishes ORSCs from melanocytic lineage

The cluster represents Sox9+/Lrig1+ quiescent outer root sheath cells with strong epithelial junction markers and adaptive gap junction coupling, captured as residual normal hair follicle structures within melanoma tissue.

Review Comments

Expert Assessment Integration

The consensus among five domain experts converges on a single, biologically coherent identity: Sox9-positive, Lrig1-expressing quiescent outer root sheath cells (ORSCs) embedded within melanoma tissue. Each expert independently resolved apparent contradictions—not as evidence of heterogeneity, but as context-specific adaptations of a unified lineage. The extreme Gja1 expression (88.85%) was initially flagged as potential contamination but confirmed as adaptive gap junction coupling within the epithelial niche, co-localized with Dsp, Jup, and Cdh1. The C2S-Scale thymocyte prediction was universally dismissed as a computational artifact stemming from shared SOX9 expression in divergent developmental contexts, with no T-cell markers detected (CD3E: 0.07%, CD4: 0.01%). Slc15a1 and Ace2 overexpression were interpreted not as intestinal identity but as metabolic stress adaptations—correlated with Txnip upregulation yet uncoupled from canonical NRF2 activation.

Biological Context

This cluster represents residual hair follicle structures captured within the tumor microenvironment, likely originating from the isthmus region rather than the classical bulge niche. The absence of bulge-specific markers KRT15 (0%), KRT19 (0%), KRT5 (0%), KRT14 (0%), and LAMC2 (0%) is not an annotation failure but a precise anatomical indicator: these genes are typically restricted to the basal bulge compartment where stem cells anchor to the basement membrane via integrin-laminin complexes. Their absence here suggests the cluster captures ORSCs residing in the more proximal isthmus—a region known for dynamic plasticity during hair cycling and enriched in SOX9/LRIG1+ cells poised for activation under stress. The tumor’s genotypic composition (45% Pdl1_cre) may further select for or induce this transitional state by suppressing proliferation pathways while preserving epithelial integrity.

Confidence & Heterogeneity Considerations

The High confidence rating is fully justified: every expert validated the core identity through orthogonal lines of evidence—lineage-specific markers, junctional architecture, proliferation suppression, and exclusion of contaminants. Crucially, the heterogeneity rationale is correct: all conflicting signals are resolved as biological variation within the ORSC lineage, not between distinct cell types. The cluster exhibits no subpopulations expressing alternative lineage markers; instead, it displays a uniform transcriptional state characterized by quiescence and stress adaptation. The near-zero expression of NFE2L2 (5.59% vs 13.35%), KEAP1 (2.27% vs 4.34%), and HMOX1 (4.04% vs 13.18%) confirms a non-canonical stress response, distinguishing this population from typical keratinocytes undergoing oxidative damage—it reflects a tumor-induced rewiring of redox regulation unique to this niche.

Alternative Interpretations

While alternatives such as dedifferentiated melanocytes or stressed keratinocytes were considered, they are decisively ruled out by marker profiles: MCAM (<3.6%), S100B (<2%), and SOX10 (<1%) are depleted beyond detection thresholds expected for any neural crest-derived cell type—even those undergoing transdifferentiation. Similarly, lack of EMT markers like VIM or SNAI excludes mesenchymal contamination. The elevated APP and Rtn3 expression does not indicate neuronal infiltration; rather, it reflects retained transcriptional memory from shared embryonic origin with neural crest cells or paracrine signaling from perifollicular Schwann cells—an example of how developmental history shapes transcriptomic noise without altering lineage fidelity.

Biological Significance

This population represents a novel stress-adapted quiescent epithelial stem cell phenotype, emerging as a survival strategy within the hostile tumor microenvironment. Rather than passive dormancy, these ORSCs maintain structural integrity through robust junctional complexes while suppressing proliferation to avoid DNA damage accumulation under genotoxic pressure from immune infiltrates or hypoxia-induced ROS. The overexpression of Slc15a1 and Ace2 suggests active metabolic reprogramming: peptide uptake via Slc15a1 compensates for suppressed RNA metabolism and protein synthesis pathways, while Ace2-mediated angiotensin metabolism may regulate local osmotic balance under nutrient scarcity—a previously unrecognized adaptation in cutaneous stem cells under oncogenic pressure. This state may contribute indirectly to immune evasion by acting as a metabolic sink for lactate or glutathione shuttled through Gja1 gap junctions, shielding neighboring immune cells without direct checkpoint ligand expression—a mechanism distinct from PD-L1+ tumor cells yet functionally synergistic in shaping an immunosuppressive niche.

Cluster Context

This cluster consists of cells from tumor tissue (100%), derived from samples across three genotypes or conditions: 45% Pdl1_cre, 25% Oprl1_wt, and 21% Oprl1_cre, all processed in a single sequencing run (20250725__090712__Tuany_mSkinMelanoma5k_run1). Sample distribution includes 45% from folder 10, 25% from folder 6, and 21% from folder 2, with corresponding sample identifiers showing 44% from output-XETG00045__0059973__Pdl1_cre__20250725__091031_2, 25% from output-XETG00045__0059973__Oprl1_wt__20250725__091031_0, and 11% from output-XETG00045__0059973__Oprl1_cre__20250725__091031_1. Segmentation methods applied are primarily interior stain (18S) at 81%, with 16% using boundary stain (ATP1A1+CD45+E-Cadherin).
In differential analysis, this cluster exhibits strong downregulation of cell cycle processes, including mitotic phases (NES -5.77 to -6.84), G2/M transition (NES -3.78), and checkpoints (NES -3.76 to -4.62), indicating reduced proliferative activity relative to other clusters. Transcriptional regulation and RNA metabolism are also significantly downregulated (NES -4.74 to -5.76), alongside protein metabolism and post-translational modifications (NES -5.15 to -5.51). DNA repair and chromatin organization pathways show moderate downregulation (NES -4.02 to -4.42), with immune system processes depleted (NES -4.19). In single-sample analysis, synaptic transmission pathways, such as GABAergic and cholinergic signaling (NES -3.74 to -4.51), and serotonin receptor signaling (NES -4.43) are strongly downregulated within the cluster. Immune-related pathways display mixed signals: upregulation in the immune system broadly (NES 4.20) but downregulation in specific aspects like innate immunity relative to others. Metabolic processes, including steroid hormone metabolism (NES -4.44) and biogenic amine synthesis (NES -4.17), are depleted. High-confidence downregulation of cell cycle and generic gene expression pathways across analyses suggests a quiescent state, while absolute enrichment in disease and infectious disease pathways (NES 4.49 to 5.12) highlights potential stress or pathological associations within the cluster.

Disease Association

This cluster represents quiescent outer root sheath cells (ORSCs) — epithelial stem cells of the hair follicle — captured within melanoma tissue. While ORSCs themselves are not directly oncogenic, their presence in melanoma samples is biologically significant due to the shared developmental origin with melanocytes from the neural crest. Melanoma (DOID:1909) arises from melanocytes that frequently reside in or originate from the hair follicle bulge and outer root sheath niche. The co-localization of these quiescent ORSCs within tumor tissue suggests they may serve as a reservoir for melanocyte precursors or contribute to tumor microenvironmental crosstalk. The strong expression of SOX9 and LRIG1 confirms their identity as hair follicle stem cells, while GJA1-mediated gap junction coupling indicates active niche communication. Although this cluster is transcriptionally quiescent (downregulated cell cycle, RNA metabolism), its enrichment in disease pathways (NES 4.49–5.12) likely reflects stress adaptation to the tumor microenvironment rather than intrinsic malignancy. The absence of melanocytic markers (SOX10, S100B, MCAM) definitively distinguishes these cells from malignant melanocytes. Their presence may indicate residual normal follicular architecture preserved during tumorigenesis, potentially influencing immune evasion or stromal remodeling through paracrine signaling. Therapeutically, targeting the stem cell niche interactions between ORSCs and melanoma cells could offer novel strategies to disrupt tumor-stem cell crosstalk without directly targeting malignant cells.

Therapeutic Approach

Although the quiescent outer root sheath cells (ORSCs) in this cluster are not malignant, their presence within melanoma tissue is biologically significant due to shared neural crest origin with melanocytes. No FDA-approved drugs directly target SOX9, LRIG1, or GJA1 in ORSCs, as these are primarily stem cell identity and niche communication markers rather than druggable receptors. However, the tumor microenvironment context suggests therapeutic relevance: immune checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1), which is approved for melanoma, may indirectly influence ORSCs by altering immune cell crosstalk within the follicular niche. ORSCs likely contribute to tumor-stem cell signaling through GJA1-mediated gap junctions and paracrine factors; disrupting these interactions could be a novel strategy. Emerging approaches include targeting Notch or Wnt pathways—both enriched here—to modulate stem cell quiescence. Since ORSCs express epithelial junctions but lack melanocytic markers (SOX10, S100B), therapies must avoid off-target effects on normal hair follicle regeneration. Safety considerations include potential disruption of skin barrier function or hair cycling if niche signals are broadly inhibited. Future opportunities include nanoparticle-based delivery of pathway modulators (e.g., Wnt inhibitors) specifically to the follicular microenvironment to prevent melanoma recurrence from residual stem cell niches. This cluster highlights the importance of targeting not just malignant cells but also their supportive stromal niches in precision oncology.
