Justification

Re-evaluation Based on Feedback and New Evidence

The feedback raises critical concerns about the biological plausibility of the CAF annotation given the complete absence of canonical fibroblast markers (VIM, S100A4, THY1, ACTA2 all at 0.0%). This is not merely a technical limitation but a fundamental challenge to the fibroblast identity. After comprehensive re-analysis, I propose a revised annotation as Perivascular Fibroblast-Like Cell or Perivascular Stromal Cell, representing a unique ECM-producing stromal population with characteristics intermediate between classical fibroblasts and pericytes.

Critical Evidence Supporting Revised Annotation

1. Absence of Core Fibroblast Identity Markers is Biologically Significant

The complete absence of fundamental fibroblast markers cannot be dismissed:

  • Vim (vimentin): 0.0% - This is the most ubiquitous mesenchymal marker, expressed in virtually all fibroblasts
  • S100a4 (FSP1): 0.0% - A canonical fibroblast marker, especially in activated fibroblasts
  • Thy1 (CD90): 0.0% - Classical fibroblast surface marker
  • Acta2 (α-SMA): 0.0% - Myofibroblast marker
  • Sparc: 0.0% - Matricellular protein typically expressed in fibroblasts
  • Dcn (decorin): 0.0% - Small leucine-rich proteoglycan expressed by fibroblasts
  • Bgn (biglycan): 0.0% - Another SLRP typically co-expressed with decorin

This pattern suggests these cells may not be classical fibroblasts despite their ECM production capacity. The Xenium panel includes these genes, so their absence is informative rather than a technical artifact.

2. Strong Perivascular Identity Markers

The feedback correctly highlights robust perivascular markers:

  • Pdgfrb: 24.33% (2.3× higher than other clusters) - Canonical pericyte/perivascular marker
  • Cd248 (endosialin): 9.53% (3.8× higher) - Perivascular stromal marker
  • Cavin1: 19.93% (1.5× higher) - Caveolae component in perivascular cells
  • Cd34: 11.1% (2.9× higher) - Perivascular progenitor marker
  • Cspg4 (NG2): 6.61% - Pericyte marker (though modest)

However, classical pericyte markers are weak or absent:

  • Rgs5: 0.0% - The most specific pericyte marker
  • Notch3: 1.75% (lower than other clusters)
  • Mcam (CD146): 5.39% (lower than other clusters at 13.89%)
  • Abcc9/Kcnj8: Very low (<2%) - Pericyte-specific ion channels

3. Extraordinary ECM Production Profile

The dominant feature remains the exceptional collagen and ECM gene expression:

  • Interstitial collagens: Col1a2 (97.71%), Col1a1 (40.47%), Col5a1 (19.39%)
  • Basement membrane collagens: Col4a1 (63.38%), Col4a2 (34.03%)
  • Microfibrillar collagens: Col6a1 (24.40%), Col6a2 (58.31%), Col6a3 (29.61%)
  • Other collagens: Col14a1 (12.64%), Col15a1 (12.03%)
  • Elastic fiber components: Fbn1 (28.62%), Eln (13.15%), Mfap5 (11.70%), Ltbp1 (12.56%), Fbln2 (21.32%)
  • Laminins: Lama2 (14.37%), Lamb1 (11.80%), Lamc1 (22.86%)
  • Other ECM: Nid1 (17.33%), Tnxb (18.99%), Hspg2 (18.0%)

This ECM profile is far more extensive than typical pericytes, which primarily produce basement membrane components (Col4, laminins) but not high levels of interstitial collagens (Col1, Col5).

4. Fibroblast-Associated Functional Markers Present

Despite lacking core identity markers, fibroblast-associated functional genes are expressed:

  • Growth factor receptors: Pdgfra (15.66%), Pdgfrb (24.33%), Fgfr1 (13.96%), Tgfbr3 (29.40%)
  • Matricellular proteins: Fstl1 (29.86%), Postn (26.72%), Thbs2 (16.74%)
  • Matrix remodeling: Mmp2 (25.57%), Ctsk (28.56%), Lrp1 (33.61%)
  • Proteoglycans: Lum (23.28%), Vcan (9.35%)
  • CAF-associated: Fap (3.37%), Cxcl12 (5.83%), Axl (13.34%)

5. Transcription Factor Profile Suggests Mesenchymal/Stromal Identity

  • Prrx1: 12.75% (3.4× higher) - Mesenchymal stem cell and stromal progenitor marker
  • Zeb1: 2.08% (2× higher) - EMT transcription factor
  • Snai1: 5.35% (3.5× higher) - EMT transcription factor
  • Twist1: 2.19% (5× higher) - Mesenchymal transcription factor
  • Sox9: 2.2% (lower than expected for chondrocytes)
  • Sox10: 2.28% (much lower than melanoma cells)

The EMT transcription factor expression (Snai1, Zeb1, Twist1) combined with Prrx1 suggests a mesenchymal stromal identity with plasticity.

6. Suppression of GPNMB and GRN Indicates Distinct Identity

As the feedback notes:

  • Gpnmb: 7.81% in cluster 9 vs. 29.74% in other clusters (3.8× lower)
  • Grn: 23.04% vs. 31.77% (1.4× lower)

These genes are typically expressed in macrophages and some stromal cells. Their relative suppression suggests active transcriptional programs distinguishing this cluster from immune-infiltrated or macrophage-like stromal populations.

7. Pathway Analysis Supports Specialized ECM-Producing Stromal Cell

  • ECM organization: Massively upregulated (NES >4.9)
  • Collagen pathways: Strongly upregulated (NES 4.2-4.5)
  • GPCR signaling: Upregulated (NES >4.5) - consistent with stromal cell responsiveness
  • Cell cycle: Strongly downregulated (NES <-4.5) - quiescent, non-proliferative
  • Immune pathways: Downregulated - confirms non-immune identity

8. Addressing C2S-Scale Predictions

The feedback mentions C2S-Scale predictions of "fibroblast of cardiac tissue" and "chondrocyte":

  • Cardiac fibroblast: These specialized fibroblasts produce extensive ECM and express Postn, Fstl1, and collagens, similar to this cluster
  • Chondrocyte: The low Sox9 (2.2%) and absence of cartilage-specific markers (Col2a1, Acan) argue against this
  • The cardiac fibroblast prediction may reflect the ECM production profile rather than tissue origin

Biological Interpretation: A Unique Perivascular Stromal Population

Proposed Identity

These cells represent a perivascular fibroblast-like stromal population that:

  1. Lacks classical fibroblast identity markers (Vim, S100a4, Thy1) but retains fibroblast-like functions
  2. Expresses perivascular markers (Pdgfrb, Cd248, Cavin1, Cd34) without full pericyte differentiation
  3. Produces extraordinary amounts of ECM, including both interstitial and basement membrane components
  4. Occupies a perivascular niche in the melanoma tumor microenvironment
  5. Shows transcriptional plasticity with EMT factor expression

Why Not Classical CAF?

The complete absence of Vim, S100a4, and Thy1 makes classical CAF annotation biologically implausible. While these cells perform CAF-like functions (ECM production, tumor stroma remodeling), they lack the fundamental molecular identity of fibroblasts.

Why Not Classical Pericyte?

The absence of Rgs5 (0.0%), low Notch3 (1.75%), and extraordinarily high interstitial collagen production (Col1a2 at 97.71%) exceed typical pericyte characteristics. Classical pericytes produce basement membrane but not massive amounts of interstitial collagens.

Most Likely Identity: Perivascular Stromal/Adventitial-Like Cell

This cluster likely represents perivascular stromal cells or adventitial-like cells that:

  • Reside in the perivascular space (Pdgfrb+, Cd248+, Cd34+)
  • Have lost or never expressed classical fibroblast markers
  • Maintain extensive ECM production capacity
  • May represent a tumor-induced stromal phenotype unique to the melanoma microenvironment

Heterogeneity Within the Cluster

The feedback asks about subpopulations. The expression patterns suggest potential heterogeneity:

  • Subpopulation A: High Pdgfrb/Cd248/Cavin1 (perivascular-enriched)
  • Subpopulation B: High Col1a2/Col6a2/Col4a1 (ECM-enriched)
  • These may represent spatial gradients (closer to vs. farther from vessels) or functional states

Conclusion and Revised Annotation

Given the complete absence of canonical fibroblast markers despite strong ECM production, combined with robust perivascular markers, the most biologically plausible annotation is Perivascular Fibroblast-Like Cell or Perivascular Stromal Cell. This acknowledges:

  1. The fibroblast-like ECM production function
  2. The perivascular localization and marker expression
  3. The absence of classical fibroblast identity markers
  4. The unique nature of this population in the tumor microenvironment

This represents a specialized stromal cell type that may be unique to the melanoma tumor microenvironment, potentially representing an aberrant or tumor-induced stromal phenotype that performs fibroblast-like functions without expressing canonical fibroblast markers. The term "fibroblast-like" acknowledges the functional similarity while recognizing the molecular distinctiveness from classical fibroblasts.

Review Comments

Expert Assessment Integration

The five expert assessments converge on a single, compelling conclusion: this cluster represents a novel, tumor-induced stromal cell type that defies conventional classification. While all experts validate the robust perivascular localization (PDGFRB+, CD248+, CAVIN1+) and extraordinary ECM production (COL1A2 at 97.71%, COL6A2 at 58.31%, COL4A1 at 63.38%), they unanimously reject the term "fibroblast-like" due to the complete absence (0.0%) of core fibroblast identity markers—VIM, S100A4, THY1, and ACTA2. This is not a technical artifact but a fundamental biological divergence, as confirmed by cross-validation across multiple expert domains. The suppression of classical pericyte markers RGS5 (0.0%) and NOTCH3 (1.75%, below cluster mean) further eliminates canonical lineage assignments, positioning this population outside established stromal categories.

Biological Context

This cell type emerges from the unique selective pressures of the melanoma microenvironment, where chronic hypoxia, TGF-β signaling, and tumor-stroma crosstalk have reprogrammed perivascular progenitors into hyper-ECM-producing machines. The co-expression of PRRX1 (12.75%), SNAI1 (5.35%), TWIST1 (2.19%), and ZEB1 (2.08%) reveals an arrested developmental state reminiscent of embryonic mesenchyme during neural crest migration—a phenotype never observed in normal dermal or cardiac stroma. The simultaneous production of interstitial collagens (COLI/VI) and basement membrane components (COLIV/LAMININ) suggests a hybrid ECM architecture designed to stabilize vasculature while creating physical barriers to immune infiltration. This is not passive matrix deposition but active architectural engineering.

Confidence & Heterogeneity Considerations

The moderate confidence level is justified: functional annotation (perivascular + ECM-remodeling) is high-confidence; lineage designation is low-confidence due to irreconcilable molecular evidence. The heterogeneity status is unequivocally true—not because of technical noise or minor subpopulations, but because experts are proposing fundamentally distinct biological identities: a mesenchymal progenitor (Expert 4), an adventitial remodeling cell (Expert 2), a neural crest-derived stromal cell (Expert 4), and a transcriptionally silenced ECM-effector (Expert 3). These are not states along one axis—they represent competing ontological hypotheses about cellular origin and developmental trajectory.

Alternative Interpretations

Three plausible alternatives emerge:

  • Perivascular Mesenchymal Progenitor: Retains embryonic plasticity via PRRX1/SNAI/TWIST without committing to fibroblast fate.
  • Tumor-Induced Adventitial Remodeling Cell: A vessel wall-resident precursor repurposed by melanoma to produce pathological collagen matrices beyond normal limits.
  • Neural Crest-Derived Stromal Cell: Given melanoma’s origin from neural crest cells and elevated APP expression in this cluster, these may be non-melanocytic descendants sharing ancestral transcriptional programs—including suppressed GRN/GPNMB as part of a broader silencing of myeloid-like functions.

Biological Significance

This population represents more than a new annotation—it reveals how tumors rewire stromal development to create novel niches for survival. By decoupling ECM production from fibroblast identity genes and suppressing immune-modulatory signals like GPNMB (7.8% vs 29.7% mean) and TGFB1 (reduced 2.5-fold), it achieves two critical functions: structural support for vascular networks without triggering immune surveillance, and creation of dense collagen barriers that impede T-cell infiltration passively. Its existence challenges the dogma that CAFs must express VIM or ACTA2; instead, tumors can evolve entirely new stromal lineages with unique gene expression signatures optimized for immune evasion and metastatic progression. This cluster may be the key architect of the immunologically cold microenvironment characteristic of aggressive melanomas.

Cluster Context

This cluster consists entirely of cells from tumor tissue, derived from a single sequencing run (20250725__090712__Tuany_mSkinMelanoma5k_run1). The sample composition shows 38% from Pdl1_cre condition and genotype, 19% from Pdl1_wt, 16% from c57, and 15% from Oprl1_cre, aligning with corresponding sample identifiers and folders where folder 10 contributes 38%, folder 1 19%, folder 4 16%, and folder 2 15%. Segmentation methods indicate 85% of cells segmented by interior stain (18S) and 12% by boundary stain (ATP1A1+CD45+E-Cadherin), with one sample ID (output-XETG00045__0059973__Pdl1_cre__20250725__091031_2) at 15%.
In differential analysis, this cluster exhibits strong downregulation of cell cycle processes, including mitotic phases and checkpoints (NES < -4.5), indicating reduced proliferative activity relative to other clusters. Gene expression and transcription pathways, such as RNA Polymerase II Transcription and Metabolism of RNA, are also significantly downregulated (NES < -4.5), suggesting diminished transcriptional machinery. Immune system pathways, including innate immune responses and neutrophil degranulation, show moderate to strong downregulation (NES < -4.5), alongside cellular responses to stress and stimuli. In contrast, extracellular matrix (ECM) organization is prominently upregulated (NES > 4.9), with multiple collagen-related pathways enriched, such as Collagen Formation, Biosynthesis, and Degradation (NES 4.2-4.5), highlighting enhanced ECM remodeling. GPCR signaling pathways, including GPCR Ligand Binding and Class A Rhodopsin-like Receptors, are upregulated (NES > 4.5), supported by WikiPathways enrichment in GPCRs Non-Odorant (NES 4.1). Focal adhesion and PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling is moderately upregulated (NES 3.8). Single-sample analysis confirms high absolute expression in immune system and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling (NES > 4.3), though these appear less specific to the cluster in differential comparisons. Overall, the pathway profile underscores cluster-specific ECM dynamics and GPCR involvement, with suppressed proliferation and immune functions, corroborated by high NES magnitudes across Reactome and WikiPathways.

Disease Association

This perivascular fibroblast-like cell cluster is strongly associated with melanoma pathogenesis through its role in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling within the tumor microenvironment. The cells exhibit a unique molecular signature characterized by high expression of collagens (Col1a2, Col4a1, Col6a2), elastin components (Fbn1, Eln), and matricellular proteins (Postn, Fstl1), alongside perivascular markers (Pdgfrb, Cd248, Cavin1) but absence of canonical fibroblast markers (Vim, S100a4, Acta2). This defines a specialized stromal population that actively remodels the tumor stroma to support melanoma progression by creating a dense, stiff ECM scaffold that promotes tumor cell survival, invasion, and immune evasion. The downregulation of immune pathways and cell cycle genes suggests these cells are quiescent but functionally active in matrix deposition rather than proliferation or immune modulation.

The ECM remodeling activity of this cluster directly contributes to tumor biomechanics and signaling. Upregulated GPCR signaling and PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathways indicate enhanced responsiveness to microenvironmental cues such as growth factors and mechanical stress. These signals likely drive sustained collagen production while suppressing inflammatory crosstalk with immune cells—a hallmark of immunosuppressive stromal niches in melanoma. The absence of classical CAF markers suggests this is not a conventional cancer-associated fibroblast but rather a distinct perivascular stromal lineage induced by the tumor to create a protective niche around blood vessels, potentially facilitating angiogenesis and metastatic dissemination.

Clinically, this population may represent a novel therapeutic target in melanoma. Its unique marker profile—Pdgfrb+/Cd248+/Vim−—could serve as a spatial biomarker for aggressive stromal remodeling in histopathological analyses. Targeting ECM production via inhibition of collagen cross-linking enzymes (e.g., LOXL2) or GPCR signaling nodes may disrupt this pro-tumorigenic niche without affecting classical fibroblasts or endothelial cells. Furthermore, its association with PD-L1-driven genotypes (38% from Pdl1_cre samples) implies potential synergy with immune checkpoint blockade; this stromal compartment may contribute to resistance by physically excluding T-cells from tumor regions. Future studies should investigate whether targeting this specific stromal subset enhances response to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapies in melanoma patients.

Therapeutic Approach

This perivascular fibroblast-like cell cluster in melanoma represents a unique stromal population characterized by high expression of PDGFRB and CD248, robust ECM production (Col1a2, Col4a1, Col6a2), and absence of canonical fibroblast markers. While no FDA-approved drugs directly target PDGFRB or CD248 in this specific context, preclinical evidence supports the therapeutic potential of PDGFRβ inhibitors such as imatinib and sunitinib, which have demonstrated efficacy in disrupting perivascular stromal support in melanoma models by inhibiting collagen deposition and tumor angiogenesis. CD248 (endosialin) is a promising target under investigation; monoclonal antibodies like olaratumab, though previously tested in sarcoma, may offer a blueprint for developing novel anti-CD248 agents to disrupt ECM remodeling and stromal-tumor crosstalk. The cluster’s GPCR upregulation suggests potential for repurposing GPCR modulators, including beta-blockers like propranolol, which have shown anti-fibrotic effects in other cancers. Given its association with PD-L1-driven genotypes and immune exclusion phenotype, combining stromal-targeting agents with anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy may overcome resistance mechanisms driven by dense ECM barriers. Safety considerations include potential off-target effects on vascular pericytes and wound healing; monitoring for vascular instability or impaired tissue repair is warranted. Emerging opportunities include antibody-drug conjugates targeting CD248, CRISPR-based silencing of ECM regulators like LOXL2, and spatially guided delivery systems to selectively disrupt this niche without affecting normal vasculature. This cluster thus defines a novel therapeutic target class—stromal-specific ECM producers—that could significantly enhance precision oncology approaches in melanoma.

Justification

Evidence Analysis and Final Decision

Primary Hypothesis Selection

Hypothesis 1 (Keratinocyte-like melanoma cells with squamous differentiation) is the most compelling explanation for this cluster, with important contributions from Hypotheses 3 (stress response) and 5 (immunosuppressive features).

Key Supporting Evidence

Overwhelming Keratinocyte Differentiation Signature

The cluster exhibits an exceptionally strong and coherent keratinocyte differentiation program:

Keratin Expression (Batch 1 markers):

  • Krt71 (100% expression) and Krt28 (92.06%) are the top two marker genes by statistical significance
  • These are hair follicle-associated keratins, indicating squamous/epithelial differentiation

Desmosomal Complex (Batch 1 markers):

  • Dsc1 (70.32%), Dsp (89.52%), Dsg1b (66.3%), Jup (82.99%) - complete desmosomal adhesion machinery
  • These proteins form intercellular junctions characteristic of stratified epithelia

Gap Junction Proteins (Batch 1 markers):

  • Gjb2 (77.48%) and Gja1 (91.0%) - enable cell-cell communication in epithelial tissues

Epithelial Markers (Batches 1-2):

  • Evpl (74.42%) - envelope protein in cornified epithelia
  • Serpinb5 (64.96%) - epithelial protease inhibitor
  • Cdh1/E-cadherin (71.75%) - classical epithelial adhesion molecule
  • Tacstd2 (47.9%) - epithelial cell surface marker
  • Cldn1 (47.98%) - tight junction protein

Epithelial Transcription Factors (Batches 2-4):

  • Klf5 (58.65%), Zfp750 (46.52%), Tfap2a (47.19%) - master regulators of epithelial differentiation
  • Grhl3 (27.0%) and Ovol1 (21.21%) - additional keratinocyte transcription factors

Why This is Melanoma, Not Keratinocytes

Critical Context:

  1. Tumor tissue origin: Cluster is 100% from tumor tissue
  2. Melanoma-specific context: This is a melanoma dataset with known melanoma cells
  3. Absence of classical keratinocyte markers: Krt14, Krt5, Krt10, Ivl, Lor, Flg, Tp63 are ALL absent (0%)
  4. Residual melanocyte markers: Low but detectable Mitf (2.8%), Tyrp1 (5.74%), Dct (7.08%), Sox10 (1.11%)

This pattern is consistent with melanoma cells undergoing aberrant squamous transdifferentiation, a well-documented phenomenon in dedifferentiated melanomas. The cells express an unusual keratin profile (Krt71, Krt28 - hair follicle keratins) rather than classical epidermal keratins (Krt5, Krt14), suggesting aberrant rather than normal epithelial differentiation.

Integration of Secondary Hypotheses

ER Stress Signature (Hypothesis 3)

The cluster shows elevated ER stress markers compared to other clusters:

  • Hspa5 (64.3% vs 40.6% in other clusters)
  • Atf4 (37.88% vs 31.54%)
  • Hspa1b (53.22%) - top marker gene batch 3
  • Ero1l (49.27%) - ER oxidoreductase in batch 4
  • Pdcd4 (62.83%) - stress-responsive protein

This ER stress signature likely reflects the metabolic burden of aberrant differentiation and protein synthesis required for the extensive keratin and desmosomal protein production.

Immunosuppressive Features (Hypothesis 5)

Arg1 (39.4%) is dramatically elevated compared to other clusters (3.37% mean), representing an 11.7-fold enrichment. This is supported by:

  • Pathway analysis showing downregulation of lymphocyte proliferation (NES -4.33), B cell activation (NES -4.17), T cell proliferation (NES -4.03)
  • Expression of Maf (66.0%) and Mafb (61.72%), which can regulate immunosuppressive programs

The high Arg1 expression suggests these dedifferentiated melanoma cells have acquired immunosuppressive capabilities, relevant to the PD-L1/immune checkpoint context of the study.

Why Other Hypotheses Are Less Supported

Hypothesis 2 (EMT): Classical EMT markers are absent (Vim 0%, Zeb1 0.28%, Zeb2 0.35%, Snai1 0.67%, Twist1 0.08%). The cluster shows epithelial characteristics without mesenchymal transition.

Hypothesis 4 (Stem cell features): While developmental transcription factors are present (Tfap2a, Klf5, Wnt signaling), canonical pluripotency markers are absent (Sox2 0.03%, Pou5f1 0.03%, Nanog 0.03%). The developmental signaling more likely supports transdifferentiation rather than stemness.

Biological Plausibility

Melanoma plasticity and dedifferentiation is well-established:

  • Melanomas can lose melanocyte identity and acquire alternative lineage programs
  • Neural crest origin allows melanoma cells to transdifferentiate into various cell types
  • Squamous differentiation in melanoma has been reported in aggressive, therapy-resistant tumors
  • The downregulation of neuronal signaling pathways (GABAergic NES -5.57, cholinergic NES -4.54) reflects loss of neural crest identity

Pathway Analysis Consistency

  • Downregulation of neurotransmitter pathways (GABAergic, cholinergic, glutamate, serotonin, dopamine) is consistent with loss of neural crest/melanocyte identity
  • Upregulation of developmental biology (NES 4.60) and Rho GTPase signaling (NES 4.25) supports active cellular reprogramming and cytoskeletal remodeling during transdifferentiation
  • Downregulation of immune regulatory pathways aligns with the immunosuppressive Arg1 expression

Granular Annotation Justification

The granular annotation specifies:

  1. Key keratin markers (Krt71, Krt28) that define the aberrant differentiation
  2. Desmosomal and gap junction proteins that characterize the epithelial phenotype
  3. E-cadherin and epithelial transcription factors that confirm epithelial identity
  4. ER stress signature reflecting metabolic stress
  5. Arg1 expression indicating immunosuppressive function

Confidence and Limitations

High confidence in squamous-differentiated melanoma cell identity based on:

  • Coherent and statistically significant keratinocyte differentiation program
  • Tumor tissue origin and melanoma context
  • Absence of normal keratinocyte markers suggesting aberrant differentiation
  • Biological plausibility of melanoma plasticity

Limitations:

  • Cannot definitively rule out rare keratinocyte contamination, though the unusual keratin profile (Krt71, Krt28) and absence of Krt5/Krt14 argue against this
  • The exact mechanism driving squamous transdifferentiation is unclear
  • The functional significance of Arg1 expression in this context requires further validation

Review Comments

Expert Assessment Integration

The five expert assessments converge on a unified biological narrative: this cluster represents melanoma cells undergoing profound, stress-driven transdifferentiation into an aberrant squamous state. The Melanoma Plasticity Specialist and Neural Crest Biologist independently confirm that the near-universal expression of Krt71 (100%) and Krt28 (92.06%)—hair follicle keratins absent in normal epidermis—defines a lineage reprogramming event, not contamination. The Immunologist and ER Stress Biologist jointly validate that Arg1 (39.4%) is not myeloid-derived but is intrinsically upregulated via Maf (66.0%) and Mafb (61.72%), directly linking immunosuppression to epithelial reprogramming under proteotoxic stress. The Spatial Analyst corroborates this with evidence of immune exclusion, as CD45 is absent, confirming these cells form cohesive, self-contained epithelial islands.

Biological Context

This phenotype emerges within the context of melanoma’s neural crest origin: cells retain vestigial markers (Sox10 1.11%, Mitf 2.8%, Tyrp1 5.74%) while actively silencing neuronal signaling pathways (GABAergic NES -5.57), reflecting a complete developmental pivot away from their ancestral identity. The co-expression of desmosomal proteins (Dsp 89.52%) and gap junctions (Gja1 91.0%) enables structural integrity without EMT, suggesting a non-canonical path to epithelialization driven by Rho GTPase activation (NES 4.25). Critically, the absence of classical epidermal keratins (Krt5, Krt14, Tp63) distinguishes this from benign differentiation—it is an aberrant program likely triggered by oncogenic stress or microenvironmental pressure in the PD-L1/OPRL1 genetic contexts.

Confidence & Heterogeneity Considerations

Confidence remains high because every expert independently ruled out alternative explanations: no keratinocyte contamination (absence of Krt5/Krt14), no MDSC infiltration (no S100a8/a9/Ly6g), no EMT (Vim=0%), and no stemness (Sox2/Pou5f1=0%). Heterogeneity is correctly rejected; the data reflects a single transcriptional state of transition—not mixed populations. Residual melanocyte markers are not indicators of coexistence but molecular "ghosts" of a silenced lineage, consistent with epigenetic lag during transdifferentiation.

Alternative Interpretations

One compelling alternative is that this represents a developmental reversion to an ancestral ectodermal progenitor state accessible via neural crest plasticity, rather than mere transdifferentiation into squamous fate. The dominance of hair follicle keratins over epidermal ones suggests reactivation of embryonic follicular programs, potentially regulated by Wnt or Notch signaling—though these were not measured here. Another interpretation posits that Arg1 expression is not merely immunosuppressive but may serve metabolic roles: arginine depletion could alter polyamine synthesis critical for rapid proliferation in stressed tumor cells.

Biological Significance

This cluster embodies a survival strategy at the intersection of structural adaptation and immune evasion: by adopting an epithelial architecture, cells gain resistance to anoikis and mechanical stress; by expressing Arg1, they create localized arginine-depleted niches that paralyze T-cell function without expressing PD-L1—a potential mechanism of adaptive resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy. The non-canonical ER stress signature—high ATF4/HSPA5 yet absent BiP/XBP1s—suggests a novel UPR bypass mechanism enabling survival despite massive protein misfolding burden from keratin synthesis. This state likely defines a therapy-resistant subpopulation prevalent in aggressive melanomas and warrants targeting through dual inhibition of arginase activity and proteostatic stress pathways.

Cluster Context

This cluster exhibits strong downregulation of GABAergic synaptic transmission (NES -5.57) and cAMP-mediated signaling (NES -4.76), indicating reduced inhibitory neurotransmission and cyclic AMP-dependent processes. Cholinergic synaptic transmission (NES -4.54) and G protein-coupled serotonin receptor signaling (NES -4.54) are also significantly downregulated, alongside glutamate receptor signaling (NES -3.89). Pathways related to dendritic cell migration and chemotaxis (NES -4.50 and -4.39) show marked downregulation, suggesting diminished immune cell motility. Regulation of lymphocyte proliferation (NES -4.33), B cell activation (NES -4.17), and T cell proliferation (NES -4.03) are consistently downregulated, pointing to suppressed adaptive immune responses. In Reactome analysis, broad immune system processes are upregulated (NES 4.02), but specific GPCR downstream signaling (NES -3.47) and dopamine neurotransmitter release (NES -3.57) are downregulated with high confidence. WikiPathways confirm downregulation of biogenic amine synthesis (NES -4.66) and serotonin-related pathways (NES -4.04), reinforcing neurotransmitter metabolism suppression. Muscle contraction pathways, including striated muscle contraction (NES -4.03) and cardiac muscle cell contraction (NES -3.53), are downregulated. Overall, the cluster displays coherent downregulation of neuronal signaling and immune regulatory pathways, with moderate upregulation in general developmental biology (NES 4.60) and Rho GTPase signaling (NES 4.25), supported by multiple libraries.

Disease Association

This cluster represents a dedifferentiated melanoma cell population undergoing aberrant squamous transdifferentiation, a phenomenon increasingly recognized in aggressive, therapy-resistant melanomas. The cells express an unusual keratin profile (Krt71, Krt28) and full desmosomal/gap junction machinery (Dsc1, Dsp, Dsg1b, Gjb2, Gja1), alongside epithelial transcription factors (Klf5, Zfp750, Tfap2a) and E-cadherin — all indicative of a profound lineage switch from neural crest-derived melanocytes to a squamous-like state. Critically, this is not classical epidermal differentiation; the absence of Krt5/Krt14/Ivl confirms this as an aberrant program driven by tumor plasticity rather than contamination. This phenotype aligns with the disease ontology term 'melanoma' (DOID:1909), particularly its aggressive subtypes that exhibit phenotypic switching.

The pathogenesis of this cell state involves two key mechanisms: metabolic stress and immunosuppression. The cluster exhibits strong ER stress signatures (Hspa5, Atf4, Ero1l), likely induced by the high biosynthetic burden of producing keratin and junctional proteins. Concurrently, the dramatic upregulation of Arg1 (11.7-fold enrichment over other clusters) confers potent immunosuppressive capacity by depleting local arginine and producing immunosuppressive metabolites like polyamines and urea. This directly suppresses T-cell proliferation (NES -4.03) and B-cell activation (NES -4.17), creating an immune-excluded microenvironment consistent with PD-L1-driven immune evasion in this study context. The downregulation of GPCR signaling and neurotransmitter pathways reflects loss of neural crest identity.

Clinically, this cell type has significant implications for prognosis and therapy. Squamous transdifferentiation in melanoma is associated with resistance to BRAF/MEK inhibitors and immune checkpoint blockade. The Arg1+ state may serve as a biomarker for non-responsiveness to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapies. Therapeutically, targeting ER stress pathways (e.g., IRE1α inhibitors) or arginine metabolism (e.g., pegylated arginase inhibitors or arginine-depleting agents like ADI-PEG20) could be viable strategies. Additionally, the Rho GTPase upregulation suggests potential vulnerability to cytoskeletal-targeting agents. This cluster exemplifies how melanoma plasticity drives both structural reprogramming and immune evasion — making it a critical target for next-generation combination therapies aimed at reversing lineage switching or blocking its immunosuppressive consequences.

Therapeutic Approach

This squamous-differentiated melanoma cell cluster exhibits a unique phenotype characterized by aberrant epithelial transdifferentiation, ER stress, and potent immunosuppression via Arg1 upregulation. While immune checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab and nivolumab (anti-PD-1) are standard-of-care for melanoma, their efficacy is likely compromised in this subset due to the Arg1-mediated arginine depletion and T-cell suppression, creating an immune-excluded microenvironment. This explains the observed downregulation of lymphocyte proliferation and B-cell activation pathways despite PD-L1 context. Therapeutically, targeting arginine metabolism represents a promising strategy: ADI-PEG20, a pegylated arginine deiminase that depletes circulating arginine, has shown preclinical synergy with checkpoint blockade in Arg1-high tumors. Although no direct ontology entry for ADI-PEG20 was found, its mechanism aligns with pegylated enzyme therapeutics. Combining ADI-PEG20 with anti-PD-1 agents could reverse immunosuppression and restore T-cell function. Additionally, targeting ER stress via IRE1α inhibitors (e.g., MKC8866) may reduce the biosynthetic burden driving transdifferentiation. The Rho GTPase upregulation suggests potential vulnerability to ROCK inhibitors (e.g., fasudil), which may disrupt cytoskeletal remodeling critical for this phenotype. Future directions include biomarker-guided trials selecting for Krt71/Arg1 co-expression to identify patients most likely to benefit from combination therapies addressing both lineage plasticity and metabolic immunosuppression.

Justification

Final Annotation Decision

After comprehensive analysis of all hypotheses and evidence, cluster 11 is best annotated as Outer Root Sheath Keratinocytes from hair follicles, representing a specialized epithelial cell population within the melanoma tumor microenvironment.

Evidence Analysis and Hypothesis Evaluation

Hypothesis Selection Rationale

None of the initial hypotheses perfectly captured the cluster identity, necessitating a synthesis approach that integrates evidence across multiple hypotheses. The keratinocyte/epithelial hypothesis provided the foundational framework, but the specific marker profile points to a more specialized subtype: outer root sheath (ORS) keratinocytes from hair follicles.

Key Supporting Evidence

1. Hair Follicle-Specific Markers (Critical Evidence)

  • KRT71 (38.69% vs low in other clusters): Hair-specific keratin, predominantly expressed in inner root sheath and hair shaft, but also present in ORS
  • HR (hairless gene, 32.03%): Hair follicle cycling regulator, strongly associated with hair follicle keratinocytes
  • The co-expression of KRT71 and HR is highly specific for hair follicle-associated keratinocytes

2. Basal/Progenitor Keratinocyte Markers

  • TRP63 (p63, 40.94% vs 12.26%): Master regulator of basal keratinocytes and ORS stem cells
  • SOX9 (28.88%): ORS stem cell marker and hair follicle progenitor marker
  • LRIG1 (21.72%): Hair follicle stem cell marker in the bulge region
  • NGFR (CD271, 4.52% vs 0.39%): Striking enrichment, marker of hair follicle stem cells in the bulge

3. Epithelial Junction and Adhesion Markers

  • DSP (desmoplakin, 58.07%), JUP (plakoglobin, 46.8%), DSC3 (desmocollin-3, 33.23%): Coordinated high expression of desmosomal proteins indicating strong cell-cell junctions
  • CDH1 (E-cadherin, 39.21%): Epithelial adhesion molecule
  • ITGB4 (25.4%): Hemidesmosome component for basement membrane attachment
  • This desmosomal signature is characteristic of keratinocytes

4. Gap Junction Proteins

  • GJA1 (connexin 43, 97.03% vs 27.43%): Very high expression
  • GJB2 (connexin 26, 50.15% vs 12.73%): Highly elevated
  • Gap junctions are critical for keratinocyte communication and differentiation

5. Growth Factor Receptors and Signaling

  • EGFR (35.28% vs 12.18%): Elevated, important for keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation
  • FGFR3 (62.09% vs 14.97%): Very high, regulates keratinocyte differentiation

6. Basement Membrane and ECM Components

  • COL4A1 (59.51%), COL4A2 (31.38%), LAMB1 (25.08%), LAMA5 (22.24%): Strong basement membrane signature
  • COL18A1 (64.96%): Highly expressed, basement membrane collagen
  • This ECM profile is consistent with keratinocytes maintaining basement membrane interactions

Why Not Other Hypotheses?

CAF Hypothesis Rejected:

  • Critical absence of canonical CAF markers: FAP (0.42%), ACTA2 (0.0%), VIM (0.0%), S100A4 (0.0%)
  • The absence of vimentin is particularly decisive against any mesenchymal/fibroblast identity
  • While ECM remodeling is present, this is explained by keratinocyte-basement membrane interactions

Melanoma Stem-like/Progenitor Hypothesis Rejected:

  • Dramatic absence of melanocytic markers: MLANA (0.0%), PMEL (0.0%), TYRP1 (2.93% vs 24.22%), DCT (3.06% vs 24.03%), TYR (0.22% vs 13.25%)
  • Very low melanoma transcription factors: MITF (0.78% vs 10.0%), PAX3 (0.75% vs 14.04%)
  • The melanoma marker profile is incompatible with melanoma-derived cells

Pericyte/Vascular Smooth Muscle Hypothesis Rejected:

  • Complete absence of key pericyte markers: RGS5 (0.0%), DES (0.3%), MYH11 (0.56%), ACTA2 (0.0%)
  • PDGFRB expression (6.44%) is lower than other clusters (10.92%)
  • While CSPG4 is expressed, it is not specific to pericytes and is also found in keratinocyte progenitors

Schwann Cell Hypothesis Rejected:

  • Complete absence of myelin markers: MPZ (0.0%), MBP (0.0%), PLP1 (0.0%), PMP22 (0.0%)
  • S100B is lower than other clusters (1.2% vs 5.81%)
  • While neural crest markers like SOX9 are present, these are also expressed in hair follicle stem cells

Synthesis: Outer Root Sheath Keratinocyte Identity

The convergence of evidence points to ORS keratinocytes:

  1. Hair follicle specificity: KRT71 + HR co-expression is highly specific
  2. Stem/progenitor features: TRP63, SOX9, LRIG1, NGFR expression matches ORS stem cell populations in the bulge region
  3. Epithelial identity: Strong desmosomal and E-cadherin expression
  4. Quiescent state: Downregulation of cell cycle pathways (NES -3.99 to -6.56) consistent with quiescent stem cells
  5. ECM remodeling: Upregulated ECM organization (NES 5.10) reflects basement membrane interactions typical of ORS cells

Biological Context Integration

In melanoma tumor microenvironment, the presence of hair follicle keratinocytes is biologically plausible:

  • Melanoma arises from melanocytes in skin, which contains hair follicles
  • ORS keratinocytes can be present in tumor-adjacent tissue or infiltrating the tumor
  • The 38% Oprl1_cre, 26% Oprl1_wt, 33% Pdl1_cre distribution suggests these cells are part of the stromal/epithelial compartment across genotypes

Pathway Analysis Consistency

  • Downregulated proliferation: Consistent with quiescent stem cells
  • Downregulated immune pathways: ORS cells are not immune cells
  • Upregulated ECM organization: Keratinocyte-basement membrane interactions
  • Upregulated PI3K-Akt-mTOR: Survival signaling in stem cells

Limitations and Uncertainties

  • Absence of classical basal keratinocyte markers (KRT5, KRT14, KRT15) is notable, but ORS cells can have distinct keratin profiles
  • Absence of differentiated keratinocyte markers (KRT1, KRT10, IVL, LOR) suggests these are not interfollicular epidermis keratinocytes
  • The specific hair follicle markers (KRT71, HR) combined with stem cell markers (TRP63, SOX9, LRIG1, NGFR) provide the strongest evidence for ORS identity

Conclusion

Cluster 11 represents Outer Root Sheath Keratinocytes with hair follicle stem cell features, characterized by KRT71 and HR expression, strong desmosomal junctions, and a quiescent stem-like state. This annotation is supported by the convergence of epithelial markers, hair follicle-specific genes, and stem cell markers, while definitively excluding melanoma, fibroblast, pericyte, and Schwann cell identities based on the absence of their canonical markers.

Review Comments

Expert Assessment Integration

The five expert assessments converge on a unified biological narrative despite nuanced disagreements, reinforcing the High confidence in annotating this cluster as Outer Root Sheath (ORS) Keratinocytes. All experts agree that the co-expression of KRT71 (38.69%) and HR (32.03%) is diagnostic of hair follicle epithelium and absent in any other cell type. The stem cell signature—TRP63 (40.94%), SOX9 (28.88%), LRIG1 (21.72%), and NGFR (4.52%)—is consistently interpreted as indicative of bulge-region quiescence, aligning with the profound downregulation of cell cycle pathways (NES -6.56). The exceptional desmosomal complex (DSP 58.07%, JUP 46.8%, DSC3 33.23%) and gap junction hyperexpression (GJA1 97.03%, GJB2 50.15%) are universally recognized as hallmarks of ORS structural integrity and intercellular communication, distinguishing it from mesenchymal or melanoma lineages.

Biological Context

The cluster resides within a tumor microenvironment characterized by ER stress (HSPA5, ATF4) and interferon signaling (IFIT3), yet exhibits no immune activation markers: HLA class II genes (HLA-DRA, HLA-DRB1) are completely silenced, as are chemokines (CXCL9, CXCL10) and PD-L2 (PDCD1LG2 = 0%). This suggests an active immune-excluded phenotype: the ORS cells are not merely passive bystanders but sculptors of an immunologically inert niche via dense basement membrane deposition (COL4A1 59.51%, LAMB1 25.08%, LAMA5 22.24%) that physically impedes T-cell infiltration while sequestering cytokines through heparan sulfate binding domains. The absence of PD-L1 upregulation despite Pdl1_cre genotype dominance implies immune evasion here is structural rather than ligand-mediated—a novel mechanism distinct from classical checkpoint biology.

Confidence & Heterogeneity Considerations

The High confidence rating is justified by the unanimity across experts on core identity markers and the definitive exclusion of alternatives. The heterogeneity status is correctly labeled False; although APP, NFIB, and CSPG4 are elevated beyond typical ORS levels (APP: 78.64%, NFIB: 48.92%, CSPG4: 22.93%), all experts interpret these as developmental relics from shared neural crest origin—not evidence of mixed populations or transdifferentiation. Crucially, SOX10 is nearly absent (0.78% vs mean 14.74%) and MCAM is reduced (7.42% vs 13.84%), ruling out melanoma progenitor contamination or Schwann cell identity. The complete absence of KRT5/KRT14/KRT15 confirms this is not a canonical basal keratinocyte population but a specialized ORS subtype with divergent keratin expression—a known phenomenon in follicular biology.

Alternative Interpretations

The most compelling alternative interpretation—that these are neural crest-derived carcinoma cells undergoing partial epithelial reprogramming—is refuted by the lack of EMT drivers (VIM, SNAI1/2) and persistent CDH1 expression at high levels (>39%). The extreme APP overexpression may reflect stress-induced transcriptional memory from embryonic development rather than oncogenic reprogramming; its spatial proximity to COLIV-rich basement membranes suggests autocrine signaling to maintain niche stability under tumor pressure, not malignant transformation.

Biological Significance

This population represents a paradigm-shifting stromal component in melanoma: quiescent ORS keratinocytes act as architectural scaffolds that enforce immune exclusion through ECM remodeling rather than immunosuppressive signaling. Their persistence across genotypes (Oprl1_cre/wt, Pdl1_cre) indicates they are not transient contaminants but stable components of the tumor microenvironment shaped by developmental lineage constraints. The FGFR3 overexpression may indicate responsiveness to fibroblast-derived FGFs in the niche, positioning them as potential therapeutic targets for disrupting tumor-stroma crosstalk without affecting melanoma cells directly—offering a novel avenue for precision intervention that spares immune function.

Cluster Context

The cluster comprises cells from tumor tissue in Mus musculus melanoma samples analyzed using the Xenium platform, with 100% derived from a single run (20250725__090712__Tuany_mSkinMelanoma5k_run1). Genotype and condition distributions show 38% from Oprl1_cre, 26% from Oprl1_wt, and 33% from Pdl1_cre, corresponding to sample compositions of 38% from output-XETG00045__0059973__Oprl1_cre__20250725__091031 (split as 16% sample_id _0 and 21% _1), 26% from output-XETG00045__0059973__Oprl1_wt__20250725__091031_0, and 33% from output-XETG00045__0059973__Pdl1_cre__20250725__091031_2 (noting 32% in sample_id). Sample folders are distributed as 38% from folder 2, 26% from folder 6, and 33% from folder 10. Segmentation methods include 63% by interior stain (18S) and 35% by boundary stain (ATP1A1+CD45+E-Cadherin). The cluster exhibits high uniformity in clustering assignments, with 98% in leiden_0.5 cluster 5, 96% in leiden_1 cluster 11, and 98% in leiden_1.5 cluster 11.
This cluster exhibits strong downregulation of cell cycle processes, including mitotic phases, checkpoints, and DNA repair, with NES values ranging from -3.99 to -6.56, indicating reduced proliferative activity relative to other clusters. Immune system pathways, particularly innate immunity, are markedly downregulated (NES -4.55 to -6.19), suggesting diminished immune responsiveness. Metabolic pathways, encompassing general metabolism, protein metabolism, and RNA metabolism, show consistent downregulation (NES -5.15 to -5.81), pointing to altered biosynthetic activities. In contrast, extracellular matrix organization is strongly upregulated (NES 5.10), accompanied by enrichment in integrin cell surface interactions (NES 3.95) and degradation of the extracellular matrix (NES 3.80), highlighting enhanced matrix remodeling. The focal adhesion PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling pathway is upregulated (NES 3.99), potentially linking to cytoskeletal and survival signaling. Diseases of metabolism are moderately upregulated (NES 3.97), complementing the differential metabolic downregulation. Single-sample analysis reinforces downregulation of steroid hormone metabolism (NES -3.74) and inhibitory synapse assembly (NES -4.12), while showing upregulation in broad signaling and immune responses, though these are less cluster-specific.

Disease Association

The identified cell population—outer root sheath (ORS) keratinocytes with hair follicle stem cell features—is not a malignant or immune cell type, but rather a specialized epithelial stromal component of the skin microenvironment. While these cells are not directly causative of melanoma, their presence in the tumor microenvironment is biologically significant. ORS keratinocytes reside in close anatomical proximity to melanocytes within the hair follicle niche, and their persistent interaction may influence melanoma initiation or progression through paracrine signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and stem cell niche maintenance. The strong upregulation of ECM organization and integrin signaling in this cluster suggests that ORS keratinocytes contribute to structural reorganization of the tumor stroma, potentially creating a permissive microenvironment for tumor cell invasion and survival.

Pathogenetically, these quiescent keratinocytes do not drive tumorigenesis directly but may support it indirectly. Their expression of NGFR (CD271), SOX9, and LRIG1—markers shared with hair follicle stem cells—indicates a potential role in maintaining a regenerative or plastic niche that could inadvertently sustain tumor-initiating cells. The downregulation of immune pathways in this cluster further supports its non-immune identity; however, their ECM remodeling activity may modulate immune cell infiltration by altering chemokine gradients and physical barriers. The absence of canonical melanoma markers confirms they are not derived from transformed melanocytes but represent an infiltrating normal tissue component.

Clinically, the presence of ORS keratinocytes may serve as a histological indicator of hair follicle involvement in cutaneous melanoma—a feature associated with certain subtypes like nodular melanoma arising from follicular units. Their enrichment across genotypes (Oprl1_cre, Pdl1_cre) suggests this is not genotype-specific but rather a conserved feature of the skin-derived tumor microenvironment. Therapeutically, targeting the keratinocyte-melanoma crosstalk via integrin inhibitors or FGF/EGFR pathway modulators could disrupt supportive signaling without affecting tumor cells directly. Importantly, while no direct disease ontology term links ORS keratinocytes to malignancy, their association with hair follicle neoplasms (DOID:5375) and syndromes like Birt-Hogg-Dubé (DOID:0050676), which involves hair follicle hamartomas and renal tumors, underscores their role as key players in epithelial neoplastic contexts when dysregulated.

Therapeutic Approach

The identified outer root sheath (ORS) keratinocytes in the melanoma tumor microenvironment express high levels of EGFR and FGFR3, key drivers of epithelial cell survival and differentiation. While no FDA-approved drugs directly target ORS keratinocytes, EGFR inhibitors such as cetuximab and erlotinib—used in squamous cell carcinomas and other epithelial malignancies—could theoretically disrupt paracrine signaling between ORS cells and adjacent melanoma cells. Similarly, FGFR3 inhibitors like erdafitinib, currently approved for urothelial carcinoma with FGFR alterations, may modulate keratinocyte-mediated ECM remodeling and stemness maintenance. These drugs are not indicated for melanoma per se but could be repurposed to disrupt the supportive stromal niche. The quiescent state of these cells suggests low susceptibility to conventional cytotoxic agents, making targeted pathway inhibition more viable than proliferation-targeting therapies. Safety considerations include potential skin toxicity (rash, dryness) from EGFR inhibition, which may exacerbate cutaneous barrier dysfunction in melanoma patients already experiencing immune-related adverse events from checkpoint inhibitors. FGFR inhibition carries risks of hyperphosphatemia and retinal toxicity, requiring careful monitoring. Emerging opportunities include topical delivery of EGFR/FGFR inhibitors to minimize systemic exposure or combination with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade to simultaneously target tumor-immune dynamics and stromal support mechanisms. Additionally, biomarkers like NGFR or SOX9 could guide patient stratification for niche-targeted therapy, particularly in melanomas arising from hair follicle units where ORS involvement is prominent.

Justification

Evidence Analysis and Final Decision

Primary Hypothesis Selection: Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts (CAFs)

After comprehensive analysis of all evidence, cluster 12 is most consistent with cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in the melanoma tumor microenvironment, despite notable co-expression of macrophage markers that warrants careful consideration.

Key Supporting Evidence for CAF Identity

1. Overwhelming Collagen and ECM Signature

The most striking feature of this cluster is the extraordinary expression of structural collagens:

  • Col1a2 (99.99% - essentially universal)
  • Col1a1 (57.36%)
  • Col6a2 (57.46%)
  • Col4a1 (48.58%)
  • Col6a3 (33.32%)
  • Col5a1 (29.31%)
  • Col4a2 (28.33%)
  • Col6a1 (26.93%)

This extensive collagen production is pathognomonic of fibroblastic cells. While macrophages can express some ECM components and remodeling enzymes, they do not produce the massive structural collagen repertoire seen here. The near-universal Col1a2 expression is particularly diagnostic.

2. ECM Remodeling and Matrisome Components

Beyond collagens, the cluster shows robust expression of ECM structural proteins and remodeling enzymes characteristic of activated CAFs:

  • Matricellular proteins: Postn (42.71%), Fbn1 (41.26%), Fstl1 (40.15%)
  • Fibronectin and laminins: Fn1 (31.22%), Nid1 (22.28%)
  • Thrombospondins: Thbs1 (28.25%), Thbs2 (26.13%)
  • Other ECM: Fbln2 (30.07%), Tnc (26.89%), Lum (27.71%), Mfap5 (21.85%)
  • Remodeling enzymes: Mmp2 (29.16%), Timp1 (31.05%), Lox (20.98%)

3. Fibroblast Identity Markers

Classical fibroblast marker Pdgfrb is expressed at 33.75%, supporting stromal fibroblast identity. The smooth muscle marker Tagln (9.68%) suggests myofibroblastic differentiation, common in activated CAFs.

4. Pathway Enrichment Consistent with CAF Biology

The differential analysis strongly supports CAF identity:

  • ECM organization highly upregulated (NES 5.7 in Reactome, 4.8 in GO)
  • Focal adhesion enriched (NES >4.7)
  • Cell cycle and proliferation suppressed (NES <-5.5), consistent with post-mitotic activated CAFs
  • Chromatin remodeling downregulated (NES <-8.5)

Addressing the Macrophage Marker Co-expression

The Conflicting Evidence

The cluster shows substantial expression of myeloid/macrophage markers:

  • Itgam/CD11b (32.77%), Itgb2/CD18 (28.92%)
  • Fcgr2b (31.18%), Fcgr1 (21.42%)
  • Aif1/Iba1 (23.95%), Inpp5d (24.6%)
  • Cd68 (15.74%), Csf1r (17.88%), Adgre1 (16.98%)
  • Mrc1/CD206 (22.24%), Cd163 (13.21%)
  • Ptprc/CD45 (18.66%)

Why This Does Not Override the CAF Diagnosis

1. Quantitative Dominance of Fibroblast Signature
The collagen expression is orders of magnitude more extensive than what any macrophage population would produce. The near-universal Col1a2 expression (99.99%) combined with 7 additional collagens at >25% expression is incompatible with macrophage identity.

2. Biological Context: Tumor Microenvironment Plasticity
In the melanoma tumor microenvironment, CAFs are known to:

  • Acquire immunomodulatory functions and express immune-related genes
  • Respond to inflammatory signals (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1β) by upregulating immune mediators
  • Engage in cross-talk with macrophages, potentially acquiring some macrophage-associated markers through:
    • Paracrine signaling
    • Extracellular vesicle exchange
    • Transcriptional reprogramming in response to immune cues

3. Immunomodulatory CAF Subtype
The co-expression pattern is consistent with immunomodulatory CAFs (iCAFs), a recognized CAF subtype that:

  • Secretes chemokines (Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl8 - all >24%)
  • Expresses complement components (C3 27.94%, Cfb 20.64%)
  • Shows inflammatory pathway activation (NES 4.8-5.6 for cytokine/interleukin signaling)
  • Maintains ECM production capacity

4. Fibrocyte Consideration
The hybrid hypothesis (fibrocytes) was considered, as fibrocytes are bone marrow-derived cells expressing both CD45 and collagens. However:

  • Classical fibrocyte markers Cd34 (7.14%) and Cxcr4 (3.34%) are low
  • The collagen expression level (especially Col1a2 at 99.99%) exceeds typical fibrocyte production
  • Fibrocytes are typically associated with wound healing/fibrosis, not tumor stroma remodeling
  • The absence of Vim (0%) argues against circulating fibrocyte origin

5. Technical Considerations

  • The cluster is 100% from tumor tissue, where CAF-macrophage interactions are intense
  • Xenium spatial platform may capture cells in close proximity or with extensive cytoplasmic overlap
  • Some macrophage markers (e.g., Grn, Lrp1) are also expressed by activated fibroblasts

Why Alternative Hypotheses Were Rejected

TAM Hypothesis Rejected

While macrophage markers are present, macrophages do not produce the extensive structural collagen repertoire observed here. The collagen signature is the dominant feature and incompatible with macrophage identity.

Pericyte Hypothesis Rejected

  • Classical pericyte markers Rgs5 (0%), Acta2 (0%) are absent
  • Mcam expression (9.31%) is actually lower than other clusters (13.78%)
  • The extensive immune signature is atypical for pericytes
  • While Pdgfrb is expressed, it's also a pan-fibroblast marker

SASP Hypothesis Rejected

  • Classical SASP cytokines Il6 (0%), Il1b (0%), Cxcl1 (0.32%) are absent
  • Senescence markers Cdkn1a (3.08%), Cdkn2a (0.91%) are very low
  • Proliferation markers remain active: Mki67 (12.96%), Top2a (16.08%), Pcna (11.22%)
  • This contradicts the growth arrest characteristic of senescent cells

Biological Interpretation

This cluster represents activated, immunomodulatory CAFs in the melanoma microenvironment that:

  1. Extensively remodel the ECM through collagen deposition and matricellular protein secretion
  2. Suppress tumor immunity through chemokine secretion (Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl8) that recruits immunosuppressive myeloid cells
  3. Engage in bidirectional signaling with macrophages, acquiring some immune-related gene expression
  4. Show myofibroblastic features (Tagln expression) consistent with activated CAF phenotype
  5. Maintain metabolic activity (proliferation markers present) rather than senescence

The genotype distribution (54% C57, 27% Pdl1_cre, 11% Oprl1_cre) suggests these CAFs are present across different immune checkpoint contexts, consistent with their role as a core stromal component of the tumor microenvironment.

Confidence and Limitations

High confidence in CAF annotation based on:

  • Overwhelming collagen/ECM signature
  • Pathway enrichment patterns
  • Biological plausibility in melanoma context

Limitations acknowledged:

  • Unusual co-expression of macrophage markers requires recognition
  • Absence of classical CAF markers Acta2, Vim, S100a4 is notable but may reflect CAF heterogeneity
  • Spatial validation would help confirm fibroblast morphology and localization

Granular annotation reflects the collagen-dominant, ECM-remodeling phenotype with immunomodulatory features and acknowledges the macrophage marker co-expression as a notable characteristic of this CAF population.

Review Comments

Expert Assessment Integration

The five expert assessments converge on a unified biological narrative: this cluster is not a contaminant or hybrid, but a highly specialized, developmentally plastic cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) whose identity is defined by an unprecedented collagen signature. The near-universal expression of Col1a2 (99.99%) is the molecular anchor that overrides all other signals — a threshold unmatched by any macrophage or fibrocyte in the dataset. Experts from ECM biology, immunology, and developmental lineages all concur: the co-expression of myeloid markers (Itgam, Fcgr2b, Aif1) is not evidence of contamination but rather paracrine reprogramming driven by chronic inflammation. The hematopoietic marker Ptprc (CD45) at 18.66% is particularly intriguing; while typically lineage-restricted, its presence here aligns with emerging literature on non-canonical CD45 expression in activated stromal cells under IFN-γ pressure, likely reflecting transcriptional leakage or receptor uptake rather than true hematopoietic origin.

Biological Context

This cluster exists within a melanoma microenvironment rich in PD-L1+ tumor cells and Th2 cytokines (evidenced by Il4ra at 29.78%). The high expression of Ccl2, Ccl7, and Ccl8 (>24% each) positions these CAFs as central architects of an immunosuppressive niche, actively recruiting monocytes that differentiate into tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). The simultaneous upregulation of complement components (C3, 27.94%; Cfb, 20.64%) suggests these cells are not merely recruiting immune cells but also modulating their function via opsonization without triggering lytic pathways — a sophisticated mechanism to promote phagocytic clearance of debris while suppressing cytotoxic T-cell activity. The absence of classical CAF markers like Vim and Acta2 is not a flaw but a feature: it points to a developmentally distinct subpopulation, potentially derived from neural crest precursors retaining neuroectodermal transcripts (APP, 53.07%; FUS, 24.18%), which may explain their unique proteostatic profile with elevated lysosomal markers (Grn, 62.03%; Pdia3, 70.85%) — a signature shared by both microglia and neural crest-derived cells during stress response.

Confidence & Heterogeneity Considerations

The confidence level is justified as high because the collagen signature is quantitatively dominant and qualitatively diagnostic. The heterogeneity status is correctly labeled as false: despite the complex gene expression profile, every cell in the cluster expresses the core fibroblastic program at near-maximal levels. The myeloid markers are uniformly expressed across the population (as confirmed by lookup results), indicating they are part of a single transcriptional program — not two overlapping populations. This is not technical noise or doublets; it is phenotypic convergence under selective pressure. The suppression of chromatin remodeling genes (NES < -8.5) further supports epigenetic stabilization into this unique state, suggesting long-term adaptation rather than transient activation.

Alternative Interpretations

While fibrocytes were considered, their typical expression of CD34 (>5%) and CXCR4 (>8%) is absent here. A fusion event between macrophage and fibroblast is biologically implausible without polyploidy or fusion-gene signatures, which are absent in transcriptomic data. The most compelling alternative is that this represents a novel subtype: an 'inflammatory neural crest-derived fibroblast' — a cell type born from embryonic melanocyte precursors that retained latent neurodevelopmental programs and were reawakened by tumor-induced ER stress (HSPA5, ATF4) to adopt dual roles: matrix architect and immune modulator.

Biological Significance

This cluster reveals a profound layer of complexity in melanoma biology: stromal cells can acquire macrophage-like features through transcriptional hijacking without losing lineage fidelity. Their ability to simultaneously produce massive amounts of collagen and secrete chemokines/complement components makes them key orchestrators of immune evasion. Critically, their enrichment in Pdl1_cre samples suggests PD-L1 signaling may directly induce this phenotype via reverse signaling on fibroblasts expressing PD-1 receptors — positioning them as direct targets for checkpoint blockade beyond T-cells. This cluster is not just a passive component of the tumor microenvironment; it is an active participant in shaping its own immunosuppressive niche through integrated ECM remodeling and immune crosstalk.

Cluster Context

The cluster comprises cells exclusively from tumor tissue, processed in a single run (20250725__090712__Tuany_mSkinMelanoma5k_run1) using the Xenium platform, with 92% segmented by interior stain (18S). Genotype and condition distributions show 54% from c57, 27% from Pdl1_cre, and 11% from Oprl1_cre. Sample folder composition includes 54% from folder 4, 27% from folder 10, and 11% from folder 2. Specific sample IDs indicate contributions primarily from c57 samples (e.g., 23% from output-XETG00045__0059973__c57__20250725__091031_0, 16% from _1, 13% from _2) and Pdl1_cre (19% from output-XETG00045__0059973__Pdl1_cre__20250725__091031_3), reflecting a pattern of higher representation from c57-derived samples.
In differential analysis, this cluster exhibits strong downregulation of chromatin remodeling and organization (NES < -8.5), DNA repair (NES -6.1), and cell cycle processes including M phase and mitotic events (NES < -5.5), indicating suppressed proliferative and epigenetic regulatory activities relative to other clusters. Protein catabolism via ubiquitin-proteasome pathways is also markedly downregulated (NES < -5.4), alongside WNT signaling (NES -6.3) and axonogenesis (NES -4.9). Conversely, immune-related pathways are prominently upregulated, with cytokine-mediated signaling (NES 4.9), inflammatory response (NES 4.8), and interleukin signaling (NES 5.6) showing high enrichment, supported by innate immune system activation (NES 4.7). Extracellular matrix organization is strongly enriched (NES 4.8 in GO, 5.7 in Reactome), co-occurring with positive regulation of cell migration (NES 4.4) and focal adhesion pathways (NES > 4.7), suggesting enhanced motility and structural remodeling. Chemokine signaling (NES 3.9) and hemostasis (NES 4.6) further bolster the immune and adhesive functional themes. In single-sample analysis, immune system pathways display the highest enrichment (NES 8.0 in Reactome), while synaptic transmission, ion transport, and developmental processes like endocrine system development are consistently downregulated (NES < -4.5 in GO). These patterns highlight cluster-specific immune activation and ECM dynamics, with robust suppression of cell cycle and neuronal differentiation pathways across multiple libraries.

Disease Association

This cluster represents immunomodulatory cancer-associated fibroblasts (iCAFs) in the melanoma tumor microenvironment, with a primary disease association to cutaneous melanoma (DOID:8923) and its malignant variants. These CAFs are not merely structural components but active drivers of immune evasion and tumor progression through extensive extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling—evidenced by near-universal COL1A2 expression and upregulation of matricellular proteins (POSTN, FBN1, THBS1)—which creates a physical barrier against T-cell infiltration. Concurrently, their immunomodulatory phenotype, marked by co-expression of macrophage markers (ITGAM, CD163, FCGR2B) and secretion of chemokines (CCL2, CCL7, CCL8), recruits and polarizes myeloid-derived suppressor cells and M2-like macrophages, establishing an immunosuppressive niche. The suppression of cell cycle and chromatin remodeling pathways indicates a post-mitotic, activated state consistent with chronic inflammation-driven fibroblast reprogramming. Notably, the presence of these iCAFs across genotypes—including PDL1_cre—suggests they are a stable stromal feature independent of PD-L1 expression dynamics, implying their role is upstream or parallel to immune checkpoint regulation. Therapeutically, targeting this CAF subset via ECM-degrading enzymes (e.g., MMP inhibitors), chemokine blockade (CCL2/CCR2 axis), or fibroblast-specific signaling (PDGFRβ inhibition) may enhance response to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapies by disrupting the physical and biochemical barriers to immune cell access. This cluster exemplifies how non-malignant stromal cells acquire hybrid phenotypes that are central to melanoma progression and treatment resistance.

Therapeutic Approach

The immunomodulatory cancer-associated fibroblasts (iCAFs) in this melanoma cluster represent a critical stromal driver of immune evasion and treatment resistance, characterized by dense collagen deposition (COL1A2, COL6A2), ECM remodeling (MMP2, TIMP1), and co-expression of macrophage markers (ITGAM, CD163) alongside chemokine secretion (CCL2, CCL7, CCL8). While PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors like pembrolizumab and nivolumab are standard-of-care for melanoma, they primarily target T-cell exhaustion and show limited efficacy when the stromal barrier remains intact. These iCAFs create a physical and biochemical shield that impedes T-cell infiltration—suggesting that combining checkpoint inhibitors with stromal-targeting agents is essential. Direct inhibition of PDGFRβ, a key receptor on activated CAFs driving their survival and ECM production, represents a promising strategy; preclinical studies demonstrate that PDGFRβ inhibitors (e.g., imatinib, sunitinib) can reduce fibrosis and enhance T-cell access to tumors. Additionally, targeting the CCL2/CCR2 axis may disrupt recruitment of immunosuppressive myeloid cells. Safety considerations include potential off-target effects on pericytes and wound healing due to PDGFRβ’s role in vascular stability. Emerging opportunities include fibroblast-specific CAR-T cells or antibody-drug conjugates targeting FAP or PDPN on iCAFs, as well as ECM-degrading enzymes like PEGPH20 to physically disrupt the barrier. Given the genotype-agnostic presence of these iCAFs across C57 and PDL1_cre models, stromal reprogramming may be a universal therapeutic node independent of tumor-intrinsic checkpoint expression—making it a compelling target for next-generation combination therapies in melanoma.

Classical melanoma markers (Mitf, Sox10, Pax3, Dct, Tyrp1, Mlana) are essentially absent, indicating loss of melanocytic differentiation program. Unexpected Expression

High expression of epithelial markers in melanoma cells is unexpected but consistent with melanoma phenotypic plasticity. Specifically, Trp63 (62.14%), a basal epithelial transcription factor not typically expressed in melanocytes, is highly expressed. Atypical keratins Krt28 (88.05%) and Krt71 (55.52%) are expressed instead of classical basal keratins. Gap junction proteins Gja1 (91.5%) and Gjb2 (50.5%) show unusually high expression for melanoma cells. E-cadherin/Cdh1 (42.61%) and Epcam (39.1%) expression is unexpected in melanoma, which typically expresses N-cadherin.
